stories.body:
Administration is suggesting an added 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total to about 40%

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump is proposing new tariffs on 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union, that would go into effect early next year, the office of the US trade representative said on Wednesday.

The administration is proposing an additional 20% tax on Chinese imports, which would bring the total tax to about 40%. Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, India, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.

In February, the supreme court ruled Trump’s so-called Liberation Day tariffs illegal. The court issued a narrow decision saying the administration had improperly used a specific emergency powers law to implement the tariffs, but did not broadly curb the president’s power to introduce new tariffs.

The administration is now using section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 as the legal basis for the new rounds of tariffs. The law gives the executive branch power to respond to unfair foreign trade practices after conducting formal investigations.

Though the White House did not give a timeline for the new tariffs, it said they could go into effect in January at the earliest. The US trade office said it would hold hearings on the new tariffs and its investigation into the unfair trade practices on 25 January.

This is the second major batch of section 301 tariffs, after the White House announced a broad slate of tariffs on more than 80 countries in July, including the UK, Mexico and Canada, saying the countries had failed to enforce bans on forced labor. A lawsuit fighting those tariffs is currently awaiting a decision in the court of international trade.

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” the US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, said in a statement on Wednesday.

“President Trump is proposing to take action to bring about the elimination of these unfair acts, policies, and practices. In doing so, we can level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”

Tariffs have proven unpopular with US voters, who handed Democrats a decisive victory in the midterm elections that will give the party control of Congress. The Yale Budget Lab estimates that tariffs currently in effect have added an additional $900 annually in costs for each US household.

The rising cost of living was the number one issue for voters ahead of November’s midterm elections, according to a Harris Poll survey for the Guardian. An earlier Harris poll found seven in 10 Americans blamed tariffs for higher prices.

Consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the Bureau of Economic Analysis announced on Wednesday, the highest rate since May and well above the Federal Reserve’s 2% annual target.

stories.title: Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
stories.summary: A review of the US president's financial disclosures shows Donald Trump's investment portfolios have regularly traded shares in the tech giant.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 7 hours ago

Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry , leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."

stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Sharp rise expected as cost pressures mount, with experts factoring in energy price cap hike and potential impact of El Niño

Food price inflation in the UK could hit 5% next year, the Bank of England has said, despite rising less sharply than feared since the onset of the Iran war.

The deputy governor Clare Lombardelli told MPs on the cross-party Treasury select committee: “Food price inflation is coming in under what we expected [it] to be, and in fact under what the industry expected it to be.”

But she said the Bank expected food price inflation to rise sharply from the current level of about 1.3%. “We think that … it will go up to 3 to 5% in the middle of next year. I mean, obviously that’s quite uncertain, but that pressure is there,” Lombardelli said.

Lombardelli was being questioned by MPs alongside other members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC).

The MPC raised interest rates by a quarter-point to 4% at its last meeting earlier this month to tackle above-target inflation, and suggested further action could be necessary.

Andrew Bailey, the Bank’s governor, said the MPC was also monitoring the potential impact of this year’s unusually large El Niño weather event on future food prices.

“There is uncertainty around this. You know, we still don’t know what the impact of this El Niño effect is going to be, for instance, because it will take time for it to manifest,” he said.

Surging oil and gas prices have pushed up the annual rate of inflation , which hit 3.6% last month, with the cost of petrol and diesel up by more than 33% over the past year.

But so far there have been fewer knock-on effects beyond energy prices. Food inflation has fallen well short of the peak above 17% seen in 2023, when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine exacerbated the supply squeeze as the global economy emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic.

Catherine Mann, an external member of the MPC who voted for a half-point increase this month, pointed to fierce competition in the food retail sector as a reason price rises had been constrained.

“We all go shopping ourselves. I can say that Aldi price match in my stores is apparent. Now, it wasn’t apparent four years ago. So that’s, I think, important,” she said.

Oil prices have fallen sharply since the Democratic party’s sweep in the US midterms brought hopes of an end to the Iran conflict, and as alternative sources of supply start to come onstream.

Bailey said if these lower prices continued, they would moderate the Bank’s predictions for UK inflation – which it had expected to peak at almost 5% next year.

“The prices are volatile … if these current prices were to stay what they are, the peak of inflation mechanically would be lower,” he said. However, Bailey and other MPC members underlined that some inflationary pressure for next year is already baked in – pointing to the 26% rise in the price cap for household energy bills due in January as an example.

The two-hour hearing underlined the divisions within the committee. The more dovish Swati Dhingra suggesting she saw this month’s rate rise as a one-off “insurance” measure, while Mann said she feared the MPC had undermined public confidence by failing to move more aggressively.

Dhingra compared the muted impact of rocketing oil and gas prices this year on the wider economy with the effects of the surge in 2022 after Russia invaded Ukraine.

At a similar point in that year, the prices of 70% of goods included in the consumer price index had risen, she said – but just 20% of prices have reacted so far this year.

But Mann pointed out that inflation had now been consistently above the Bank’s 2% target for five years.

“If we let inflation expectations drift away from 2% in the longer term, then monetary policy is going to have to work harder, meaning a higher rate for longer,” she said, adding: “The optimal response is to hike more and sooner.” The MPC’s next rate-setting meeting is on 17 December.

Published 25 November 2026

Six sitting members have been returned to Sark's Chief Pleas after the Sark general election recorded its highest voter turnout in 20 years.

Members Helen Plummer, Patrick Dewe, Nick Moloney, John Guille, Karl Rang and Joseph Perrée were among the successful candidates following the 73.67% voter turnout.

They were joined by Andrew Leaman, Thomas Lalor, Helen Sturman and Elliott Osborn.

Sitting member Carol Cragoe lost her seat, while candidates Tomaž Slivnik, Alan McKendry, Charlotte Golding, Daniel Golding and Christian Bravery were also unsuccessful.

The 73.67% voter turnout came from an electoral roll of 395 people and was up 16 people on the last by-election.

Of the total votes, 7% were done by proxy.

There was one spoilt paper as voting took place in the Island Hall and grounds on Wednesday.

Nine of the seats are available for a four-year term and one seat for a two-year term, after one conseiller was deselected due to non-attendance at three consecutive statutory meetings of the Sark government earlier this year.

stories.body:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.

On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart that Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.

Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian: “Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking. Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket.

“There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites, and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including taking intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to Earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to reach another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronaut.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and it has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade.

In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme . The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025, Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

US lawmakers have moved to try to extend the life of the ISS, citing China’s “permanent human presence in low Earth orbit” through Tiangong. Progress on turning that proposal into law has been slow. Nasa has said that after the ISS it will be “one of many customers in a robust commercial marketplace in low Earth orbit”.

The ISS was heralded as a symbol of post-cold war cooperation, but renewed cooperation with Russia seems “unlikely”, said Andrew Jones, a journalist specialising in China’s space programme.

While Tiangong is smaller than the ISS, China is understood to be preparing to double its size, “likely with the end of the ISS in mind”, Jones added. “These developments could allow China to expand its international engagement, and potentially space tourism. With the ISS nearing the end of its life and the future of western commercial space stations uncertain, China could for a time have the only permanently crewed outpost in low Earth orbit.”

China has long signalled its interest in developing Tiangong as an international hub. China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outline “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station. European and Chinese astronauts previously trained together with a view to a visit to Tiangong, but that cooperation ended for political and budgetary reasons, Jones said.

Curcio said he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out opportunities to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

stories.body:
Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.

Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.

He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”

Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.

A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.

Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”

Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report , The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.

The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.

“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.

Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.

“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”

Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”

The Chinese embassy has been approached for comment.

An Interpol spokesperson said: “Interpol knows Red Notices are powerful tools for law enforcement cooperation and is fully aware of their potential impact on the individuals concerned, which is why Interpol has a number of systems in place to avoid misuse of our systems, and these have been significantly strengthened over the last few years.

“Interpol’s constitution affirms the Organisation’s neutrality. Under Article 3, Red Notice requests must not be of a predominantly political, military, religious or racial character.”

stories.title: Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU
stories.summary: The Reform UK leader reunites with businessman Arron Banks in support of the Keep Britain Out campaign.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Nigel Farage and Arron Banks previously worked together during the 2016 EU referendum as part of a pro-Brexit campaign

Published 5 hours ago

Nigel Farage has helped launch a new campaign against the UK rejoining the European Union.

The Reform UK leader offered his support to Keep Britain Out, which sees him reunite with his Brexit-supporting ally Arron Banks - who co-founded the Leave.EU campaign during the 2016 referendum.

Farage was the first MP to sign the campaign's "Pledge for Britain". This contains "10 commitments" for elected officials to abide by, including opposing rejoining the EU, its single market or customs union.

The campaign was launched as Prime Minister Andy Burnham explores closer ties with the EU, after he agreed a deal with the bloc covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Burnham has argued that Brexit has done "more harm than good" and has suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

But he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

On Monday, Burnham said there was "no fixed destination" on the talks with the EU, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Speaking at a press conference on Wednesday, Farage said the 2016 referendum was the "most divisive thing I have seen in families, in communities" and he hopes the next general election "kills this stone dead".

He told reporters: "I didn't pick this fight, the prime minister has picked this fight. As far as I was concerned it was done and dusted.

"But if battle has to be joined I will join it gleefully. What he's doing is madness, it's not necessary."

Farage said Keep Britain Out would be a "forward-looking, positive campaign about how Britain can be richer, more productive" outside the EU.

There are 10 issues listed on the pledge card, including asking signatories to "oppose mass migration" and support the country's farming and fishing industries.

Farage suggested he expects other Reform MPs and candidates to sign the pledges.

Banks said he wants pro-leave MPs to support them, adding: "We hope some Labour MPs will see sense and sign it and even Conservatives."

Asked if he is funding the campaign and to what extent, Banks said a "whole series of donors" have been "back in touch".

He added: "The last campaign was also funded by the British public, so I'm not going to go into who's donating what at this stage."

The launch of Keep Britain Out follows the formation of another anti-EU campaign called Stay Out , which has received support from Lord Gove - the chairman of the Vote Leave campaign in 2016.

Meanwhile, the European Movement is helping launch a rival campaign to rejoin the EU, called Get In.

stories.title: New York and California Age Gating Rules Go Into Effect in the New Year
stories.summary: Come January 2027, everyday social media browsing in two of the country's largest states will look noticeably different. In California, AB 1709 (2026), AB 1043 (2025), and SB 976 (2024) are slated to take effect on January 1, 2027. Meanwhile, state attorney general regulations for New York’s Stop Addictive Feeds Exploitation (SAFE) for Kids Act take effect on January 25, 2027. EFF has opposed these laws across legislatures , regulatory proceedings , and the courts . The core problem is simple: age-gating mandates trade away everyday user privacy and free expression under the guise of safety, while pushing platforms to gather even more personal data on users. What California’s Rules Say Three interlocking California laws take effect on January 1, 2027, reshaping how platforms handle age checks and design features for young users. First, SB 976 (2024) requires verifiable parental consent before platforms can offer algorithmic feeds or nighttime notifications to anyone under 18. Second, AB 1709 (2026) goes even further by outright banning "addictive features," including personalized recommendation algorithms, autoplay, and endless scroll, for users under 16, even with parental permission. Third, the Digital Age Assurance Act (AB 1043, 2025) mandates age-assurance checks across devices (operating systems) and apps, serving as the enforcement backbone for those restrictions. Together with the California Attorney General’s proposed rules on SB 976 , which outline age-gating methods, accuracy, circumvention, and parental consent, these laws force platforms into a two-tier design that walls young people off from basic content-discovery tools, puts everyone's privacy at risk to prove their age, and has already drawn First Amendment lawsuits from social media companies against both SB 976 and AB 1709 . For example: rather than minimizing corporate surveillance and data collection by passing stronger privacy laws, the SB 976 regulations encourage companies to evaluate behavioral patterns, collected user data, digital interactions, and metadata to estimate age (Sec. 561(a)(2)), alongside location data collected for other purposes (Sec. 565). Good privacy laws should discourage collecting that information in the first place, not reward broader tracking. Nvidia's shares fall 5% at the open

Nvidia’s shares are dropping at the start of trading in New York, as the rally following the return of Jensen Huang yesterday subsides.

Nvidia has fallen by 5.5% in the first couple of minutes of trading, to $155.87. That erodes a small portion of yesterday’s 32% surge.

The chipmaker’s stock is under pressure amid criticism of Huang’s return from both Republicans and Democrats.

Niall Hearty, partner and regulatory lawyer at legal firm Weightmans, warns that reinstating Huang could backfire:

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. It seems extremely premature amid ongoing investigations by the SEC, Nvidia’s Board, the FBI and the Department of Justice. “It is understandable for a company facing this level of reputational turmoil to want to restore stability as quickly as possible. Huang’s return may have temporarily reassured investors, but a recovery in the share price does not resolve the underlying questions about governance and accountability.

Closing summary

Time to wrap up…

The sell-off in US tech stocks has resumed, as Monday’s relief rally following the reappointment of Jensen Huang to run Nvidia quickly faded.

Shares in Nvidia are down 7.7% at $152.35, wiping out around a third of Monday’s jump.

Anthropic , the frontier AI firm which floated last week, are down 9.75% at $79.08, meaning anyone who took part in its IPO (priced at $83 a share) is facing a loss.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, says:

double quotation mark “The loss of the $83 IPO price is a major development, coming so swiftly after the listing. By comparison it was a month before SpaceX suffered the same fate. Launching a major IPO in the midst of one of the biggest tech selloffs of recent times was never going to be great timing, but there was a growing sense of ‘now or never’. Huang’s return seems to have amplified the instinct to sell, given his love for open source models rather than the paid version, and absent a broader market recovery it seems Anthropic is fated to struggle for now.”

This is pulling the wider US market into the red, with the Nasdaq Composite now down 2%.

That has punctured an early feeling of relief in the markets, where Asia-Pacific bourses generally rallied today .

Stocks are sliding amid a backlash to the decision to reappoint Huang, under pressure from the White House.

Democratic senator Ruben Gallego said Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO sends a message “that the national security of this country is not as important as your relationship with president Trump.”

And Bernie Sanders has warned AI firms not to expect a bailout if their investments go wrong.

Huang will make several several appearances on Capitol Hill next week where skeptical lawmakers from both parties will grill Huang over his ties to a woman that some in the intelligence community have said was a spy for China

Our US Politics Live blog is keeping tabs on the latest developments:

The rapid expansion of AI data centre construction could exacerbate the US housing shortage by drawing workers away from homebuilding.

Oxford Economics has estimated that up to 45,000 additional workers would be employed in residential construction across the 10 states with the highest data centre spending had employment trends followed those elsewhere in the country.

Matthew Martin , senior US economist at Oxford Economics , explains:

double quotation mark “Data centre projects appear to be bidding up wages. “As data centre demand shows little sign of slowing, the wider premium may make it harder for homebuilders to compete for workers.”

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On Monday 30 November, join Dan Milmo , Professor Dame Wendy Hall , Stuart J. Russell and Alexandra Birch-Mayne as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only.

Book tickets here or at guardian.live

The S&P 500, the flagship US share index, is down 0.4% in early trading at 7,206 points.

But.. the Dow Jones Industrial Average is up 0.4%. reaching 49,795 points. Twenty three of the 30 stocks on the DJIA are up, while Nvidia (-5.5%) is the top faller.

The tech-focused Nasdaq index has opened lower too – it’s down 1.8% at 23,661 points.

Analog Devices (-15%) are the top faller, followed by chipmaker AMD (-10.1%) and SanDisk Corporation (-9.2%).

Anthropic's shares tumble below IPO price

Oof! Anthropic’s share price has tumbled below the level at which the frontier AI company sold shares to investors last week, in its record-breaking float.

Anthropic’s stock has dropped by 8.3% at the start of trading, to $80.34, below the $83 IPO price.

This may sour demand for AI-linked stocks, warns Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

She explains:

double quotation mark A drop below $83 so quickly after its IPO could also weigh on the future earnings reports of its largest backers. For example, if Anthropic’s share price falls sharply, then Google and Alphabet, which hold just under 30% of the stock, could take a hit to their bottom lines. So far, Alphabet and Amazon are posting relatively small losses on Tuesday, but these could worsen if Anthropic’s share price continues to decline.

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang’s reinstatement is already raising eyebrows and prioritising short-term stock market valuation above serious national security concerns has the potential to backfire. It seems extremely premature amid ongoing investigations by the SEC, Nvidia’s Board, the FBI and the Department of Justice. “It is understandable for a company facing this level of reputational turmoil to want to restore stability as quickly as possible. Huang’s return may have temporarily reassured investors, but a recovery in the share price does not resolve the underlying questions about governance and accountability.

Bernie Sanders: Taxpayers will not bailout Big Tech oligarchs.

Democratic senator Bernie Sanders has warned US tech companies not to expect a bailout if their AI investments turn sour.

Posting on X , Sanders says:

double quotation mark One thing must be made certain: If the AI bubble bursts, taxpayers will not bailout Big Tech Oligarchs. Not tomorrow. Not next year. Not ever. If AI companies fail, Big Tech Oligarchs must bail them out, not taxpayers. Our message to these multi-billionaires is simple: If you take out a loan, pay it back. Don’t come begging to taxpayers to bail you out.

WSJ: US prepares to raise tariffs on China and other countries

Fears of a new US-China trade war are rippling through the markets today too.

The Wall Street Journal are reporting that the US is preparing to raise tariffs on China and dozens of other countries that the Trump administration argues are harming American companies by supporting their own domestic industrial production, according to people familiar with the plans.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could release the results of a tariff investigation into the industrial subsidies of China, the European Union and 14 other nations later this week, the WSJ adds…..

Bank of England policymaker Megan Greene has warned that UK interest rates need to keep rising, unless there is a “miraculous” breakthough in the Middle East conflict.

Speaking in London today, Greene – one of the more hawkish members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee – warned that the BOE is “a little bit behind the curve now.”

She explained:

double quotation mark “I think it’s appropriate to tighten policy further unless there’s a miraculous turnaround in data or in the war.”

The City money markets indicate there’s an 84% chance that the Bank rises interest rates at its next meeting, in mid-December.

Most stock markets in the Gulf region posted gains today, taking their cue from Wall Street yesterday, and then Asia-Pacific markets overnight.

Saudi Arabia’s ⁠benchmark index gained 0.4%, while Dubai’s main share index rose by 0.8%, ​ Abu Dhabi’s market finished 1% higher, and Qatar posted a 0.75% rise.

Meta launches AI assistant Muse - are you planning to use it?

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta is launching its Muse AI assistant in the UK and is encouraging users to let it loose on their apps – and the high street.

Muse has been a hit in the US and is ranked first and second respectively on Google and Apple’s free app store, having been downloaded millions of times.

Muse can be used as an app or directly within Meta’s WhatsApp messaging platform. Meta invites users to give their assistant a name, a look and a personality, so they can talk to it as well as assign it tasks such as sending an email, booking travel or buying festive presents.

Meta says:

double quotation mark “From doing the Christmas shopping and searching for a cheaper energy deal, to sorting the school calendar … Muse can get it done for you.”

So… we’d like to know if you have plans to try Muse, or if you’re already a user. Let us know here :

Meanwhile in the bond markets, the UK has paid a record high price to sell inflation-linked bonds.

Britain’s Debt Management Office sold £3.75bn of an index-linked gilt which matures in 2049, at a real yield (the return after inflation) of 2.5235%. That, Reuters has calculated, is the highest for a syndicated sale since records began in 2005.

This chart from Deutsche Bank shows how the AI/tech selloff of recent weeks has been was one of the bigger declines of recent years:

But, Deutsche Bank’s Henry Allen points out that there are ‘clear differences’ with the other big risk-off moves of the last decade:

First, there wasn’t a sudden and fundamental reassessment of the growth outlook, like when the pandemic began in 2020, or during the Liberation Day selloff of 2025.

Second, there wasn’t a meaningful data deterioration, or even much deterioration at all, as happened in summer 2024, or in the 2015-16 selloff.

Third, there wasn’t a hawkish repricing like 2022. Admittedly, further rate hikes are priced in, but even more hikes were priced in early October when the S&P 500 and the NASDAQ hit their record highs. So that factor hasn’t changed.

If Nvidia’s shares do indeed drop when trading begins, it will take a slice out of President Trump’s wealth.

Donald Trump made up to $15m (£11.5m) on his holdings of Nvidia stock after the US chipmaker’s share price soared on the surprise return of Jensen Huang as chief executive .

That’s based on the US president’s financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics indicate he might have owned as many as 370,000 shares in Nvidia as of 30 September, the latest available data, in news first reported by the Financial Times.

The US dollar, which hit a 19-month high yesterday, has dipped by 0.3% against a basket of currencies.

That weakness is helping the pound – it’s up half a cent at $1.3088, up from a one-year low yesterday.

Elsewhere in the markets, Anthropic is at risk of falling below the level at which it sold shares to investors last week.

The frontier AI company’s stock is down 5.6% in premarket trading at $82.74, which would take it below its IPO price of $83 a share.

Anthropic also missed out on yesterday’s rally, and dipped slightly on Monday.

Duncan Ferris, analyst at Freetrade , says

double quotation mark “Jensen Huang has stolen Anthropic and [co-founder] Dario Amodei’s thunder. The massive 31% comeback rally sparked by his Nvidia homecoming has turned retail investors’ heads more than one of the biggest IPOs of all time.

Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs

Published 25 November 2026

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".

But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.

Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.

Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.

"The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs."

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.

The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

stories.body:
The Hillsborough disaster in 1989 ultimately claimed the lives of 97 Liverpool fans. In the weeks that followed, South Yorkshire Police reviewed its officers’ written accounts before passing them to the official inquiry.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel later found that 164 statements had been substantially changed. In 116 of them, comments critical of the force were removed or altered. In 2021, two former officers and the force’s solicitor were tried over those changes. The case collapsed. The judge ruled that the original inquiry wasn’t a statutory one, and the police had no legal duty of candour there.

The public office (accountability) bill, known as the Hillsborough law , currently in the House of Lords, is meant to close that gap. Covering up to 1.9 million public servants , it would require authorities and officials to act with “candour, transparency and frankness” towards inquiries and investigations. Breaching that duty with the aim of obstructing them would be a crime. The bill also creates a new offence of misleading the public, with a maximum sentence of two years in prison.

Honesty has been one of the seven principles of public life since 1995. Hillsborough shows what can happen when a moral duty may be ignored at little cost. But once honesty becomes a legal duty, someone has to decide what it requires. That’s much harder than it sounds.

Honesty is more than not lying

Research on public health communication shows that official messages can fall short of honesty without anyone telling a lie. They might use true statements to create a false impression, which is known as paltering . For example, they can leave out the size of a benefit or the harms, strip out uncertainty, or present risks in whatever form looks most persuasive.

Imagine a council official is asked at an inquiry whether they were warned that a block of flats was unsafe. They reply: “I never received a report saying the building was unsafe.” That may be strictly true. But suppose they had received several emails from residents and a fire officer raising concerns about the building’s fire doors. Nothing they said was false, yet the inquiry would come away with the wrong picture.

The Hillsborough statements fit the same pattern: the deception lay in what had been taken out.

The bill seems to accept this. Its test for “seriously improper” conduct refers to dishonesty “whether by means of falsehood, concealment, obfuscation or otherwise”. It says an “act” includes “an omission or a course of conduct”. And the duty of candour requires officials to correct “any errors or omissions” in what they have already told an inquiry.

But the bill uses the word “dishonesty” without defining it. Nor does it say what counts as “misleading”. That’s important because the line is blurry.

Every statement leaves something out. The duty of candour asks officials to provide information that’s “relevant to the inquiry or investigation”, but someone still has to decide what’s relevant. Not every omission is a cover-up.

The problem grows when the evidence is incomplete or disputed. To show that someone misled others, a court needs something to compare their statement with. Should that be the truth as it later emerged, or the best understanding at the time? Early in a public health emergency, for example, officials often have to speak before the science is settled.

This is why the difference between misinformation and disinformation matters. Misinformation is false or misleading content shared without meaning to deceive, whereas disinformation is spread on purpose. An official may give an inaccurate account because they were wrongly briefed, or may not have realised a detail mattered. That’s a failure, but not necessarily dishonesty.

Can honesty really be enforced through the law?

The bill deals with this through what lawyers call the “mental element” of an offence. To be guilty of misleading the public, officials must “act with the intention of misleading the public” or be “reckless as to whether their act will do so”. They must also “know, or ought to know, that their act is seriously improper”.

An act is only seriously improper if it “involved dishonesty that was significant or repeated” on a matter of significant public concern, caused or risked harm, and departed significantly from proper conduct.

This leaves courts with a hard task. Proving intent means piecing together what an official knew and believed at the time. Omissions are especially hard to prove. A prosecutor must show that the official had the information, understood that it mattered and chose not to share it.

Draw these boundaries too narrowly and the selective editing seen after Hillsborough could slip through again, because every sentence left in was technically true. Draw them too vaguely and officials may say less, hedge everything and send every statement through lawyers.

Criminal law also has to be clear enough for people to know in advance what’s forbidden. Honesty is a tricky concept, so it’s likely the Hillsborough law will be difficult to enforce.

The Hillsborough law already accepts that dishonesty can mean “concealment” or “obfuscation”, not just “falsehood”. What it doesn’t yet do is say where honest selection ends and dishonest concealment begins. Peers still have a chance to fix this by defining “dishonesty” and “misleading” in the bill or its guidance.

For public servants bound by the law, there is a practical lesson. “Did I say anything false?” is the wrong question. A better one is: “Will the people I’m speaking to come away with an accurate picture?”

stories.title: Johannesburg has had 101 mayors over the last 140 years: new book reviews the good times and the bad
stories.summary: South Africa’s local government elections in November 2026 drew attention to the role of mayors in municipal government, particularly in Johannesburg. However, Johannesburg’s mayoralty has a long history, with more than 100 mayors having occupied the chair. Christopher McMichael and Philip Harrison have just published a book, Johannesburg’s Mayors: 140 Years of Making and Breaking the City . Harrison answers questions about it. You wrote the book amid a deepening governance crisis. How does the book speak to this? The book doesn’t try to solve – or even dissect – the current crisis . Instead, it steps back to view Johannesburg and its governance through the long lens of history. Cities swing between growth, crisis and stagnation; a single snapshot never tells the whole story. We think history offers hope: circumstances shift. Taking the long view matters for another reason too. Cities are the product of a complex layering of multiple processes with different time horizons. Johannesburg’s crumbling infrastructure is a prime example. stories.body:
South Africa’s local government elections in November 2026 drew attention to the role of mayors in municipal government, particularly in Johannesburg. However, Johannesburg’s mayoralty has a long history, with more than 100 mayors having occupied the chair. Christopher McMichael and Philip Harrison have just published a book, Johannesburg’s Mayors: 140 Years of Making and Breaking the City . Harrison answers questions about it.

You wrote the book amid a deepening governance crisis. How does the book speak to this?

The book doesn’t try to solve – or even dissect – the current crisis . Instead, it steps back to view Johannesburg and its governance through the long lens of history.

Cities swing between growth, crisis and stagnation; a single snapshot never tells the whole story. We think history offers hope: circumstances shift.

Taking the long view matters for another reason too. Cities are the product of a complex layering of multiple processes with different time horizons. Johannesburg’s crumbling infrastructure is a prime example. While the past decade’s unstable coalitions have accelerated the decay, essential assets like water, power and road infrastructure are built to last 30 years or more – meaning their current state reflects decades of neglect.

Understanding history transforms how we experience the present.

What were the good years, and what were the bad?

One group’s golden age may be another’s darkest hour. This was, for example, the case in the 1950s and 1960s when the white middle class was realising the benefits of an American-type suburban lifestyle while the Black residents of townships were experiencing heightened state repression.

Nevertheless, some periods are associated with narratives of progress, and others with crisis or stagnation. The optimism in the late 1930s is a case in point.

The Great Depression was followed by a mining boom, with the central business district going high-rise, and new infrastructure laid out across the city. Johannesburg celebrated its golden jubilee in 1936 with the Empire Exhibition , cementing its status as a new and prosperous City of Empire.

Another period of optimism, for white Johannesburg at least, was the early 1970s. The United Party-controlled city council declared an era of civic progress with the construction of a vast network of motorways, the opening of the Carlton Centre as Africa’s tallest building, and a grand new civic centre.

The celebratory mood, of course, ended when the youth in Soweto rose in revolt in June 1976 .

Other moments of hope came in the early 1990s, as the political impasse of the previous decade ended, although the transition was turbulent. The 2000s saw at least a decade of rapid economic growth, though governance controversies persisted.

But there were certainly bad times: the South African War (1899-1902); a bitter struggle between white capital and white labour which culminated in the Rand Rebellion ; two world wars, the influenza pandemic, the Great Depression, and the shock of the Afrikaner nationalist victory of 1948.

The 1980s may have been the city’s low point. A conservative coalition of the National Party and the Independent Ratepayers Association resisted desegregation. It planned to celebrate Johannesburg’s centenary in 1986, but the then president, P.W. Botha, declared a nationwide state of emergency .

The transition in the 1990s was a roller coaster, ending with a financial crisis that nearly bankrupted the city. Over the past ten years or so, the city has seen unstable coalition governments, deteriorated service delivery, and increasing corruption, along with the COVID-19 pandemic and a stagnant economy.

It is a complex story of hope and despair, driven by an entanglement of local and national factors, but it does suggest a city of some resilience.

Why does the mayor matter in all of this?

In the colonial and apartheid years, mayors were ceremonial, elected for single-year terms, with governing left mainly to council committees. Mayors generally acted as a stabilising force, mediating in back rooms between competing interests.

From 2000, with the introduction of the executive mayoralty , mayors mattered far more directly. They led the executive branch and could drive a vision for the city.

From 2019, mayors had to cede power to coalition partners to remain in office. The city administration became a patchwork of fiefdoms.

Mayors, whether ceremonial or executive, make the complexity of city governance visible to the public. However, the mayor is only one of many actors in city administration. Bureaucrats, councillors, union heads and many others play crucial roles.

While we have used the mayor as a lens into city administration, we recognise its limitations. The book tries to contextualise the work of mayors within a much wider landscape of change.

Were there good mayors, and what measures define success?

Good and “bad” are subjective concepts. But we do have a definition of “good” for the colonial and apartheid eras, and for the post-apartheid period.

Before 1994, a “good mayor” was one who pushed the bounds of convention towards a fairer society. White Joburg society was quite conservative overall, and a radically progressive politician was unlikely to become mayor. Nevertheless, there were individuals who tried in their limited ways: Edwin Orlando Leake, who was concerned with housing opportunities for African people; Maurice Freeman, who defended Indian people from discriminatory legislation; Max Goodman, who defied police orders in engaging with protestors; Alec Jaffe, who tried to protect vulnerable tenants from unscrupulous landlords; Monty Sklaar, who promoted multi-racialism in council events.

The most consequential “good mayor” may have been Johannesburg’s first woman mayor, Jessie McPherson, elected in 1945 and representing the Labour Party. She clashed with segregationists and was subjected to a travel ban by the national government for 15 years.

The good mayors were outnumbered by the bad ones, who entrenched civic exclusion and local prejudice.

This leaves us to ask what a good mayor may be in the post-apartheid period; perhaps one who put the promise of making citizens’ lives better into effect.

The first black mayor, Isaac Mogase, served during the transitional period of the 1990s, and with his integrity and steady demeanour, provided confidence in local government. Amos Masondo, the first executive mayor of metropolitan Johannesburg, benefited from ten years of office, but his discipline, sense of duty and consistent administrative action, even if humdrum at times, was revealed in visible implementation. The transformation of Soweto during his mayoralty was a case in point. Parks Tau introduced progressive city policies, but implementation was limited as he lost the election to Herman Mashaba after five years.

Mashaba, in turn, promised to turn the city into a construction site within 12 to 18 months , but he underestimated the political and technical requirements for achieving this. After Mashaba, a quick succession of eight mayoralties followed (excluding one declared illegal by the high courts).

Based on your sweep of the city’s history, what takeaways do you offer?

We don’t offer explicit takeaways. But we can draw a few suggestions from our work.

One concerns the mayoral system itself. The indirectly elected executive mayor was quite successful in the first 15 or so years of post-apartheid rule. But not anymore.

Because of the instability created by coalition governance, the mayoralty needs a rethink. There are at least two options here.

The first would be to adopt a system of directly elected executive mayors, separating the mayor from the chaos of coalition politics.

Alternatively, some form of non-executive mayoralty could be considered. The mayor would be enjoined to remain above party politics and be a unifying figure.

stories.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
stories.summary: The post FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.body:
Rx Roulette

A ProPublica investigation last year found the Food and Drug Administration failed to regularly test generic medications that doctors warned about or drugs coming from factories with serious quality and safety violations.

The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.

Read More

Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.

“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.

A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.

ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector , a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.

Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer . All but one passed every test.

The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”

In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.

In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”

Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.

“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”

ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.

“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”

stories.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
stories.summary: The post Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul appeared first on ProPublica .

stories.body:
A top House Democrat with oversight of the Smithsonian Institution affirmed the agency’s independence and told ProPublica she’ll investigate any political pressure coming from the White House.

A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

Read More

Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.

“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”

Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.

“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.

Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.

Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.

Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter . “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”

“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote .

Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.

“Over my dead body,” he wrote .

stories.title: Why Accountability Cannot Depend on Political Power
stories.summary: The International Criminal Court has ruled that Myanmar has committed genocide. The United States has sanctioned the ICC. Which approach will prevail? The post Why Accountability Cannot Depend on Political Power appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Students participate in class in a shelter in the camp on October 28, 2019 in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh. 27 year old Rohingya refugee Shamima Bibi is currently running 16 schools for women in different tents around the camps. (Allison Joyce/Getty Images)

This month, two international courts have faced tests that expose a central weakness in the international legal order. In October, the United States imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court as an institution , extending earlier measures against its judges and prosecutors. On November 19, the International Court of Justice delivered its judgment in the genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar, finding that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Together, these developments raise an uncomfortable question: does accountability under international law depend on the political power of the state concerned?

In law, the answer should be no. The international legal system rests on the principle of sovereign equality between states , enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations . All states are bound by the same rules and obligations, whatever their size or their political, economic, or military weight. In practice, however, whether a violation is followed by consequences depends not only on its gravity but also on the balance of power, and on whether influential states are willing to cooperate with international institutions.

The weakness lies less in the absence of legal rules than in the limits of enforcement. Judgments of the International Court of Justice are binding on the parties, but the Court has no independent enforcement arm. Article 94 of the UN Charter allows a party to refer non-compliance to the Security Council, which may make recommendations or decide on measures to give effect to the judgment. That route is vulnerable to politics: the permanent members retain the power of veto . The best-known illustration is Nicaragua v. United States. After the ICJ ruled against Washington in 1986, the United States vetoed a Security Council draft resolution calling for compliance . A mechanism designed to support the Court’s rulings can therefore be blocked by the very state against which the judgment was delivered.

The Gambia v. Myanmar demonstrates another side of the problem. In 2019, The Gambia, a small West African state, brought proceedings alleging that Myanmar had violated the Genocide Convention in its treatment of the Rohingya. The Court indicated provisional measures in 2020 and upheld its jurisdiction in 2022. On November 19, 2026, it delivered its judgment on the merits and found that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya during the 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State. The Court also found violations of Myanmar’s obligations to prevent and punish genocide and to enact the necessary legislation to give effect to the Convention.

This is a landmark legal finding. But a judgment, however significant, is not the same as accountability. Its practical effect will depend on whether Myanmar complies and whether other states are prepared to support implementation.

The International Criminal Court, which prosecutes individuals rather than states, faces pressure of a different kind. The October measures followed earlier U.S. sanctions on its judges and prosecutors . The Court has strongly rejected the institutional sanctions, describing them as an attempt to obstruct its work. Its ability to continue operating matters, but resilience should not obscure the principle at stake. The independence of an international court depends not only on legal texts but also on the political environment in which it operates. It should not hinge on the goodwill of the most powerful states, particularly when the Court’s work touches their interests.

Sanctions are another tool used in the name of accountability, and research on their effectiveness is more nuanced than the headlines suggest. A 2024 review by Daniel Drezner finds that economic coercion can be more effective than scholars once believed, while also highlighting substantial unintended consequences. Sanctions can impose heavy costs without changing a state’s behaviour, and ordinary people often bear much of the burden. Their effects vary with the objective, design, and degree of international cooperation behind them. Imposing costs is not the same as securing accountability. The contradiction is especially stark when a tool intended to enforce international norms is directed at the institution charged with applying them.

These problems do not harm only the states directly concerned; they weaken the international system as a whole. When the prospect of accountability varies with a country’s influence, confidence in the impartiality of international institutions erodes. International law becomes less able to regulate relations between states and more likely to be seen as an instrument shaped by political alliances and strategic interests.

The result is not simply selective enforcement. It is a loss of confidence in the idea that international obligations apply equally.

States can help address this problem without creating entirely new institutions. Those that support the ICC can take practical steps to protect its independence and ensure that sanctions do not obstruct its mandate or the work of those cooperating with it. Members of the Security Council can also consider commitments not to use the veto to block action in response to non-compliance with ICJ judgments. Such measures would not eliminate political influence, but they could make it harder for power to determine whether international law has consequences.

The judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar demonstrates that international courts can make consequential findings, including against states accused of grave violations. But its significance will be measured not only by what the Court has declared but by what happens next. International law cannot guarantee that every judgment will be enforced immediately. It must, however, insist that accountability does not become a privilege reserved for states with less political power. A legal system in which the likelihood of enforcement varies with the strength of the state concerned risks losing one of its most important foundations: the confidence that it is a common framework governing all states rather than a tool whose effectiveness depends on the balance of power.
