stories.title: Two Banks, Two Reckonings: What Paraguay and Brazil Share
stories.summary: Corruption plagues Latin America's right-wing politicos. The post Two Banks, Two Reckonings: What Paraguay and Brazil Share appeared first on Foreign Policy In Focus .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Paraguay's President Santiago Pena pose for a photo during a world leaders' summit on ending the Gaza war on October 13, 2025 in Sharm El-Sheikh, Egypt. (Suzanne Plunkett - Pool / Getty Images)

Earlier this month, Paraguay’s Senate removed President Santiago Peña. All 44 senators present voted to oust him over the collapse of a digital bank that froze the accounts of nearly half the population, a day after the lower house impeached him unanimously. He was placed under house arrest that evening, and the next day a judge ordered him held in pretrial detention at a military facility. He is charged with breach of trust and administration for personal gain; on November 13, prosecutors added a criminal association charge , accusing him of leading a scheme with five former central bank directors to shield Ueno from scrutiny . Peña denies wrongdoing, and his lawyer says that he will plead not guilty.

The bank was Ueno. It had about three million customers , roughly 60 percent of Paraguay’s adults, and held more than $800 million in public funds, including about $380 million from the state pension and health fund. Regulators moved in after its solvency ratio fell below half the legal minimum. Peña remained a business partner of the conglomerate that owns Ueno until March 2025, though the bank says he was never a shareholder. Prosecutors allege that, as president, he pushed state entities to deposit public money in Ueno despite concerns about its health, and that two Ueno loans of about $500,000 in 2024 helped pay for his mansion. Bank executives have been arrested, and the former central bank chief, Carlos Carvallo, who once ran Ueno, is also charged.

This was a second embarrassment for the Latin American far right after the loss of Flavio Bolsonaro in the Brazilian elections at the end of October. Peña was a key ally of Donald Trump. His business-friendly economic model was touted by neoliberal admirers like Argentina’s Javier Milei . Peña and Bolsonaro don’t just share a political affinity. They both have faced similar financial scandals.

Flávio Bolsonaro is currently under investigation for the Banco Master scandal in Brazil’s central bank liquidated Banco Master on November 18, 2025, and the collapse triggered a payout of nearly $7.7 billion from the credit guarantee fund, the largest in its history. The Federal Police’s Operation Compliance Zero has since arrest ed banker Daniel Vorcaro’s father and the former president of the public Banco de Brasília, and Senator Ciro Nogueira has also been a target. Leaked messages show Flavio asking Vorcaro for 134 million reais for a film about his father, Jair Bolsonaro (under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence). The younger Bolsonaro calls the funds he received—approximately half of what he requested—private money for a private movie.

The scandal certainly dominated the presidential campaign, but it did not likely decide the result. Although directly implicated, Flávio Bolsonaro outperformed the polls in the first round, casting himself as an outsider at a time when the banking scandal seemingly affected the whole ruling class. A Datafolha poll found Brazilians split on whom the scandal tarnished more: 34 percent said the left, 27 percent the right.

The shared lesson is that a fast-growing bank can sit close to political power while regulators look away. In Paraguay, government deposits in Ueno rose to about 29 percent of its deposits after Peña took office. In Brazil, Banco Master’s license was approved under Jair Bolsonaro’s government, yet the scandal reached justices and politicians across the spectrum.

Both countries also remember what a bank freeze can do. In Brazil, in 1990, President Fernando Collor de Mello froze balances above 50,000 cruzados novos, and the stock market fell more than 20 percent as the state seized savings. Today’s crises come from private banks, and the response has been arrests and impeachment.

Paraguay’s new president, Pedro Alliana, comes from the same political machine. He rose through the Colorado Party faction led by former president Horacio Cartes, whose U.S. sanctions over alleged corruption, which he denies, were lifted last year. Alliana has confirmed holding a certificate of deposit of about $640,000 at Ueno, and the lower house rejected a motion to impeach him. No charges against him have been reported, and holding the deposit does not by itself show involvement. Analyst Andrew Nickson doubts the case will reach the powerful, saying that “only scapegoats are likely to suffer long-term sentences.”

Marc Ostfield, the U.S. ambassador to Paraguay from 2022 to 2025, argues that Ueno’s collapse exposed a political machine built around Cartes and his protégé Peña, in which public deposits and pension money flowed to friendly banks, Ueno and the Cartes-linked Banco Basa, while Washington overlooked the warning signs because Paraguay was a useful ally. Strategic alignment, he says, is not the same thing as democratic resilience. Cartes reportedly backed Peña’s removal, and the new vice president, Antonio Barrios, is another longtime Cartes ally, so the power structure may be largely intact.

The financial picture has also darkened. Central bank president Jorge Schreiner told AFP that losses could reach $1 billion in the worst case. The deposit guarantee fund has advanced roughly $650-700 million to move the accounts of about 1.8 million depositors to other banks, with payouts of up to about $18,000 per person, and Schreiner says that the fund will absorb the first loss. Bonds Ueno issued abroad are not protected by law. Ueno has assets worth $1 billion or more, but valuing them will take one to two months , and an IMF mission is expected in December. Officials said earlier in November that nearly 95 percent of savers had been compensated, yet about $800 million in public money, including pension funds, remains at risk , and the labor minister says that up to 7,000 people lost jobs at companies tied to the bank. Alliana has pledged to recover the pension money, promising that retirees will be paid .

The test is conviction, not arrest. Brazil’s probe has drawn complaints of selective leaks, and Paraguay’s prosecutors were criticized for seeking dismissal of the case against Cartes. Still, in both countries the people who lost access to their money did not stay quiet, and the institutions that were supposed to protect them have started moving. That is the first condition for trust to return.

stories.title: War Reveals a Global Food System Tethered to Fossil Fuels
stories.summary: The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout. Read more on E360 →
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A pile of sulfur at an oil refinery in Cartagena, Spain. Sulfur, a byproduct of refining, is needed to make phosphate fertilizer. Angel Garcia / Bloomberg via Getty Images

ANALYSIS

The Iran war has shuttered refineries in the Persian Gulf and throttled the production of sulfur, which is critical for making fertilizer needed to feed the world. The crisis, expected to raise grocery prices, hints at an unintended consequence of the fossil fuel phaseout.

By Fred Pearce • November 24, 2026

Facebook

Twitter

LinkedIn

Email

Millions of farmers around the world are living in fear that their crop yields will falter in the coming months. They blame the Iran war, which has reduced supplies of the phosphate fertilizer vital for a successful harvest by 40 percent and raised its price beyond the reach of many.

But few farmers will likely know that their reliance on Persian Gulf states for much of their phosphate fertilizer is an outgrowth of a global effort more than 30 years ago to banish a major environmental scourge — the sulfur emissions from power plants that caused acid rain.

Those efforts required oil and natural gas refineries in the Gulf and elsewhere to strip sulfur from their products. That waste sulfur swiftly became the go-to feedstock for making sulfuric acid, the world’s most widely used industrial chemical, and one that is essential when processing phosphate rock to make phosphate fertilizer. Sulfur prices tumbled and, unable to compete, almost all the world’s sulfur mines shut. Soon, nearly half of internationally traded sulfur was being supplied by refineries in the Gulf. Or it was until those supplies were cut off in 2026.

Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries.

There isn’t yet any reliable data on crop yields following the fertilizer drought: Most crops are still in the ground. But farmers from Brazil to India to southern Africa await with trepidation the impact on their upcoming harvests.

The rest of the world should be equally concerned. Analysts expect the crisis will cut crop yields in 2027 and beyond, raising food prices everywhere for years to come. The World Food Programme warns that, in combination with El Niño , the shortage could bring hunger to at least an additional 49 million people.

Meanwhile, analysts warn that the potential impact of the sulfur crisis on fertilizer production is likely to be just a foretaste of what will happen as the world phases out fossil fuels. An end to refining oil and natural gas would also halt the supply of waste sulfur at a time when demand is set to increase due to greater need for fertilizer and for refining metal ores for the fast-growing batteries market, says Mark Maslin, a geographer at University College London who has tracked the trade.

“My concern is that green tech outbids the fertilizer industry for the limited, more expensive sulfur supply,” he says, “creating an issue with food production, particularly in developing countries.”

A farmer spreads fertilizer on his land in Indian Kashmir. Firdous Nazir / NurPhoto via AP

Using waste sulfur from refineries to make sulfuric acid should be a textbook example of how circular economies work, with one industry’s discards becoming the feedstock for another. Tens of millions of tons of waste sulfur from refineries is used in the manufacture of everything from rubber tires to paper. Before the war, the fertilizer industry absorbed more than half of the world’s available sulfuric acid to extract phosphorus from rocks and make a product that helps to feed the world. Sulfuric acid is also used to extract copper, nickel, and cobalt from ores to make the batteries that run electric vehicles — a critical part of international efforts to reach net-zero carbon emissions by midcentury.

And yet that green virtue in 2026 turned into a liability. During the Iran conflict, damaged production plants and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the main shipping route from Gulf refineries to sulfur markets, cut off 45 percent of the world’s trade in this strategically vital waste product. (While Gulf producers have been able to export some oil and natural gas through pipelines to the Red Sea, there are no pipelines that can handle dry, solid sulfur.)

This sudden sulfur shortfall has caught governments and producers without a Plan B, says MacDonald Amoah, an analyst of critical minerals for the Payne Institute for Public Policy at the Colorado School of Mines. Because sulfur has been regarded as a waste product, it has been little monitored by trade bodies. As it happens, this industrial material, essential for feeding the world, has no strategic reserves.

Many fertilizer producers have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, can no longer pay for the product.

In the 1980s, acid rain was a headline-grabbing environmental scourge. Emissions of sulfur dioxide from power stations burning sulfur-rich fossil fuels turned the rain across Europe and much of North America as acidic as lemon juice. Forests from the Appalachian Mountains to the Carpathians in Eastern Europe lost foliage and died; acid-drenched soils released toxic metals, killing fish in rivers and lakes.

The scourge was high politics, too. Canada’s environment minister complained to a visiting Ronald Reagan that his nation’s damaged forests and lakes were at the end of a “gigantic exhaust pipe” that began in the eastern United States. Swedish and Norwegian governments blamed British power stations for their hundreds of fishless lakes.

Governments eventually acted, requiring the scrubbing of sulfur dioxide from power station flue gases. Power companies in turn demanded that refiners supplying oil and natural gas remove the sulfur at source. The result of this international clean-up was a vast new waste stream of elemental sulfur that soon found a market as a feedstock for manufacturing sulfuric acid.

By century’s end, the world was awash with cheap waste sulfur. The market price had fallen by 80 percent, forcing mines from Sicily and Mexico to the salt domes of Texas out of business. Today, more than 95 percent of the world’s sulfur comes from oil and natural gas refineries, and almost half of international trade is through the Strait of Hormuz.

Cargo ships anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran. Amirhosein Khorgooi / AP Photo

Most discussion about the resource implications of the Iran war has concentrated on disruption to the Gulf’s oil and natural gas exports. But the war has also hindered the production of the two most critical fertilizers in the world: nitrogen-based ammonia, which is made in the Gulf using hydrogen extracted from natural gas, and phosphate fertilizer, whose manufacture requires sulfur extracted from hydrocarbon refining. The conflict has cut the amount of nitrogen supplied to farmers by about a quarter but phosphate supplies by 40 percent.

As the war has progressed, the supply of sulfur has continued to shrink. In May, China, the world’s largest exporter of sulfuric acid, banned sales to foreign manufacturers to protect its own fertilizer supplies. Then in August, Ukrainian drones struck Gazprom’s Astrakhan gas processing plant, knocking out 60 percent of Russia’s sulfur production.

With supplies cut and prices up by more than a third, sometimes exceeding $1,000 per metric ton, much of the sulfur that has been available has been snapped up by the mining industry, which can afford the higher prices. The price hike has left phosphate fertilizer producers in a bind. Many have shut down because their ultimate customers, farmers, cannot pay for the product. Mosaic, one of the world’s biggest manufacturers, more than halved its U.S. production in 2026 and has announced plans to shut one plant for six months starting in December. “Without affordable sulfur,” production superintendent Hector Mier said last month, the company was “forced to curtail production. That means less fertilizer for farmers and less food grown in American farmland.” Saudi and Brazilian plants have also closed.

As less fertilizer is added to soils, says an analyst, there will be an “erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries.”

Brendan Rice, an agribusiness analyst for the Washington, D.C.-based International Food Policy Research Institute, warns that as less phosphate fertilizer is added to soils, there will be “a slow-rolling erosion of agricultural productivity in many countries” stretching through 2027 and beyond.

The first clear signs of the downturn may emerge in the next three months with the harvest of rice in India and Thailand, soy in Brazil, and corn in southern Africa. Amoah says it will “lock in grocery inflation for years.”

What will happen if the Gulf conflict continues to restrict sulfur supplies?

There is no immediate prospect of a revival of sulfur mining. Only two mines remain open: the Osiek Mine in southern Poland and the Kawah Ijen volcano on the Indonesian island of Java, where a few hundred intrepid miners armed with hand tools clamber down into the crater to dig out yellow blocks of elemental sulfur, which they haul to the surface in bamboo baskets. Neither mine could quickly increase production, analysts say. And a widespread reopening of closed mines would be a costly and risky enterprise when Gulf production of cheap sulfur could resume at least as quickly.

A miner gathers sulfur from Kawah Ijen, an active volcano on the Indonesian island of Java. Oscar Espinosa / SOPA Images / LightRocket via Getty Images

There is sulfur stockpiled at a few refineries — notably some 10 million metric tons around tar-sands deposits in the Canadian province of Alberta, some of which is sent to fertilizer manufacturers in Canada and the U.S. But scaling up distribution quickly for the international market would be challenging. “Every tonne must be excavated off the block, trucked to a melting site, melted, formed, and railed to Vancouver for vessel loading,” says Fiona Boyd , a director of London-based Acuity Commodities. “[It’s] a lengthy and expensive process.”

Experts predict that Gulf supplies of sulfur will eventually resume. But that will only postpone the day, says Maslin, when the world faces a long-term sulfur crunch as demand rises while supplies falter.

On the demand side, most observers expect a rapid increase in the use of sulfuric acid as more metals are refined to make batteries. And as the world’s population continues to rise, feeding more people will also likely require more sulfur to make more phosphorus fertilizer. Overall, Maslin sees the market growing by around 60 percent to 400 million metric tons by midcentury.

Farmers could reduce their use of synthetic fertilizers by nourishing their soils with animal manure and farm waste.

But at the same time, he says, supply is set to crash as the world’s energy system decarbonizes, with consumption peaking and then falling sharply over the next three decades, slashing the production of sulfur waste at refineries. In 2022, Maslin and his University College London colleagues calculated that shifting away from fossil fuels “could create a shortfall of sulfuric acid as large as 320 million [metric tons], or 130 percent of present-day production.”

The supply crunch would drive up the cost of sulfur, Maslin said. Then, as now, farmers — and the world’s food supply — would be the likely losers.

To address the shortfall, farmers could reduce their dependence on both nitrogen and phosphate fertilizers by nourishing their soils organically. Animal manure and organic farm wastes are rich in both chemicals. But few agriculturalists expect such methods to do more than moderate rising demand for synthetic fertilizer — and the sulfur needed to make it.

So where will the sulfur come from? We could go back to large-scale mining. Unlike some strategic materials, the world is not short of geological sulfur. It is the 13th most abundant element in the Earth’s crust, found in volcanoes, salt domes, and in sedimentary deposits created by the evaporation of seawater.

A tractor spreads fertilizer on a soybean field in Goias, Brazil. Mateus Bonomi / Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

But Maslin warns of the risks. “Direct mining of elemental sulfur is dirty, toxic, [and] destructive.” To minimize the damage, he says, “the world needs to cut demand by recycling and using alternative industrial technologies that avoid intensive use of sulfuric acid.” Widespread commercial recycling of sulfur has potential. Sulfuric acid is a major component of widely used lead-acid batteries, for instance. In the U.S. it is widely recycled along with lead.

Another approach is to cut demand for sulfur’s biggest use — making phosphate fertilizer — by recycling the phosphates found in human sewage, which is where much of the material used to grow our food ends up.

More than half the world’s population is now connected to sewage systems. Sewage sludge from treatment works may contain industrial contaminants but is generally considered safe for application to cropland and often sold or given to farmers in developed countries, notably the U.K. and the U.S. Sludge incinerators in Japan and Germany sell their leftover ash, still rich in phosphates, either to farmers or to fertilizer manufacturers. Willem Schipper, a Dutch consultant in industrial chemistry, calculates that current sewage systems worldwide could deliver around a million metric tons of phosphates each year. That is roughly 3 percent of what is mined each year, but it would trim the need for both sulfur and phosphate, a rock that is itself in increasingly short supply.

By removing phosphates from raw sewage at treatment works, recycling would also reduce the environmental impacts of high levels of phosphates in rivers, where the chemical spurs the growth of plants and algae that block sunlight from penetrating the water and lower oxygen levels. So, while one version of a circular economy might falter as fossil fuels are sidelined, another, smaller circular economy could emerge.

stories.title: The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta
stories.summary: The post The Shenzhen Summit Supplants Yalta appeared first on NOEMA .
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A world made safe for spheres of influence.

Nathan Gardels is the editor-in-chief of Noema Magazine. He is also the co-founder of and a senior adviser to the Berggruen Institute.

Pundits who dismissed the Shenzhen summit as a mere photo-op lacking substance missed the point. The significance of the conclave was precisely its enframing symbolism, showcasing a new world in which the rules-based order has been supplanted by spheres of influence accommodating each other.

The city of Shenzhen itself is a prism through which we can observe today’s power relations and the evolution of events over recent decades bringing us to this point.

Unplugged Computers in China’s Future Tech Hub

I first visited Shenzhen in 1986, arriving there by tram from Hong Kong and walking across the mainland border. There was barely any bustle, no crowds or traffic and a couple of tall buildings at the most. At our modest hotel, a squatting gardener was clipping the grass with a pair of scissors. The place still exuded the languorous vibe of the fishing village of 30,000 it had been not long before it was designated a “special economic zone” by Deng Xiaoping to attract foreign capital and technology.

On an inspection tour of sprouting industrial parks with then-former California governor Jerry Brown, our hosts proudly showed us what they called a tech hub. What then passed for “data centers” were cavernous, virtually empty warehouses with scores of desktop computers on worktables gathering dust — none were even plugged in.

What seemed embarrassing at the time turned out to be beyond impressive 40 years later. Shenzhen today is a literally glittering technopolis of 20 million people regarded as China’s “Silicon Valley” where Huawei, Tencent, DJI and BYD are all located. It is the center of gravity of China’s AI battle with the United States.

The invitation to visit had come some years earlier from Xi Zhongxun, then Party chief of Guangdong province (where Shenzhen is located) and the father of China’s current leader, Xi Jinping. The elder Xi had come to California in 1980 looking for investment in the special economic zone as a key platform of Deng’s policy of “reform and opening up” to the world. On that visit, he met Gov. Jerry Brown and toured the state, including stops at tech sites in the then-fledgling Silicon Valley (Apple and Intel were about it in those days) and Disneyland, where he gamely shook hands with Mickey Mouse.

Years later in 2012, when Brown was governor again for a second time, Xi Jinping, then-vice-president of China on his way to the top, visited California. The irony was not lost on either leader when the governor inquired whether China was interested in helping finance California’s bullet train, already in the works for nearly 20 years.

A Chinese delegation later met with the governor at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills to discuss possibilities, but the idea never panned out. Those who had once come cup in hand to the Golden State now offered financing terms too tough to abide. By 2026, China had built a 30,000-mile network of bullet trains spanning its vast country. California and the U.S. still have yet to build one.

On that 1986 trip to China, Brown and I also met at Zhongnanhai, the secluded leader’s compound in Beijing, with the ideology chief and youngest member of the ruling Communist Party Politburo at the time, Hu Qili. In a wide-ranging conversation that touched on topics from the “spiritual pollution” of Western influence to Tibetan Buddhism, Hu noted that the Chinese military had reduced its forces by one million soldiers. Many military installations, he said, were converting to commercial applications in light industry and heavy-truck production. Several military aircraft plants were now making refrigerators and motorcycles.

To this, Brown quipped, “If the army is making refrigerators, you must think the polar bear [what the Chinese called Russia] is hibernating.” Laughing, Hu simply replied that since Russia “couldn’t even consolidate control of Cambodia, it is only inviting great trouble to try anything with China.”

Opening then to America while hostile to an ebbing Soviet empire, Hu insisted that “China’s armed forces are sufficient to resist hegemonist efforts from the bear if they come.”

By the time I saw Hu again in 1988, Mikhail Gorbachev had come to power in the Kremlin, attracting some sympathy among reformers in China and inspiring a growing youth movement with his ideas of perestroika and glasnost. Enough of a thaw was in the works that Hu asked me to convey “fraternal greetings” to Aleksandr Yakovlev, then the Soviet party’s main reformist thinker, on my next stop in Moscow. Read Noema in print.

“The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.”

The Tiananmen Turn

It was in that atmosphere that Gorbachev visited Beijing in May 1989 and met with Premier Zhao Ziyang as tensions with the authorities were mounting on Tiananmen Square. In the wake of the student massacre that June, the liberal-leaning Zhao was purged for revealing “state secrets” to Gorbachev by telling him that Deng, who would order the repression, remained the power behind the throne even though he had formally retired. Hu was also purged.

This was a “ludicrous accusation,” Gorbachev told me later. The real issue, as he saw it, was his advice that the student occupation should be defused politically through negotiation, not force. “I was confident a political solution could be found. I was wrong, unfortunately,” the last Soviet leader lamented.

Deng had drawn the line on Party control that Gorbachev was erasing in Moscow. Deng’s open palm on the economy clenched into an iron fist on political reform. Ever since, Gorbachev’s “new thinking” has been vilified in Beijing as a recipe for the collapse of the Party-state, and something to be avoided at all costs.

A World Safe For Spheres Of Influence

When Vladimir Putin emerged in the tumultuous years after the Soviet collapse, China’s sympathy with a more amenable Russia returned. As the post-Cold War years wore on, the “hegemonist threat” for China shifted to America, even as it prospered from the relationship.

In the end, China’s leaders came to strategically favor a trusted autocrat ruthlessly obsessed with dominating his own neighborhood over a meddling America endlessly endeavoring, in their minds, to subvert China’s governing system and keep the nation down. Party ideologues, Xi above all, are convinced that the American political class, implicitly if not explicitly, concurs with Bill Clinton’s remark when he was president that China was on “the wrong side of history.” Like many others in those days, Clinton wrongly presumed trade winds would blow open the society.

With a militarily mighty but economically feeble and dependent Russia at its side, China’s leaders have grown more confident in their capacity to contain America in a world made safe for spheres of influence.

The few words spoken for public consumption at the Shenzhen summit about zones of “civilizational values” and the primacy of state sovereignty over international law were code for the long-standing views of Xi and Putin, which the American president has now openly embraced.

Tech Trips The Thucydides Trap

At the first meeting of the Berggruen Institute’s 21st Century Council with Xi Jinping in 2013, the Party leader boasted that “we have never been closer to realizing the dream of Chinese rejuvenation” after the long climb back from colonial humiliation — invoking that history as if it were yesterday.

As Xi sees it, far from being on the wrong side of history, only the firm hand of the Communist Party could have brought the Middle Kingdom to where it is today and can take it where it must go tomorrow.

In 2015, then Premier Li Keqiang launched a “Made in China 2025” campaign with the goal of conquering the latest technologies from electric vehicles and batteries to artificial intelligence within a decade. Xi sees this conquest as rocket fuel for the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation, which he is determined to ensure does not fall behind the West and invite domination by outside forces, as it did during the Ming and Qing dynasties of the late 19th Century.

Strategists in Washington across the partisan landscape see China’s unrelenting resolve to reach its goals as an existential threat to America’s technological supremacy, and all that implies in terms of military might and geopolitical sway.

At our 2013 meeting, Xi pointedly raised an historical reference to “the Thucydides Trap,” whereby a rising power inevitably runs into conflict with an established power, only to say China would seek to avoid it. By now, though, it is clear that of all the contested issues between the U.S. and China, technology is most likely to trip the trap. The Nvidia episode is but one skirmish in a larger battle.

Shenzhen Supplants Yalta

If I were to have a conversation with the ideology chief on the Politburo today, as I had with Hu decades ago, here is what I would imagine him saying: “We have demonstrated we can go head-to-head with America on AI and technology. Today our military is reinvigorated. We have the largest navy in the world and are scaling up our nuclear arsenal toward parity with the U.S. and Russia. To be sure, America remains a formidable foe with the legacy of hegemonist ambitions. But let’s be serious. It is crumbling within. Its aging systems are plagued by outages. It can’t even build one bullet train.”

For Xi, hosting both leaders of the other great powers in Shenzhen, where China’s tech prowess is on full display, is the ultimate icing on the cake of rejuvenation. The one key power left out of the 1945 Yalta talks that shaped the international order in the dying days of World War II is now setting the agenda for what comes next.

stories.title: What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry
stories.summary: The post What China’s Gene-Editing Deaths Reveal About Its Biotech Industry appeared first on NOEMA .

stories.body:
Regulation alone won’t fix the conditions that have earned China the reputation of the “Wild East.”

Jane Qiu is an independent science writer in Beijing.

BEIJING — In March 2023, four-year-old Mei in Shanghai was diagnosed with a rare genetic mutation linked to developmental delay and autism-like traits. Although her condition was mild and she improved with therapy and special education, her parents remained worried about her future. Hopeful for a cure, they paid Qiu Zilong, a renowned neuroscientist at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and his team $860,000 to develop a customized gene therapy. The treatment, which used adeno-associated viruses to deliver gene editors to the brain, had been approved by Xinhua Hospital, a leading hospital for rare diseases.

On March 24, 2025, trillions of viral particles carrying gene editors were injected into Mei’s spinal cord. She soon developed a fever and kidney failure and died within days. A year later, Qiu’s team published its preclinical findings in Nature, which Chinese media hailed as “a world-class breakthrough.” Mei’s death and her family’s financial support were not mentioned.

Deaths in clinical trials are not unusual. What is shocking are the regulatory lapses revealed by an investigation published this July in Science and subsequently corroborated by a separate investigation conducted by the Shanghai municipal government, which released its findings last week. The treatment’s consent form, for instance, didn’t warn of the possibility of death. The hospital had approved treatment before toxicology findings showing liver and kidney damage in monkeys that received similar treatments. And, among other crucial omissions, the researchers failed to disclose Mei’s death.

Apparently, this was not an isolated incident. Several researchers told me that Chinese hospitals commonly fail to disclose adverse events. On Aug. 5, STAT reported another death in a gene-editing trial led by Shanghai-based HuidaGene, an incident that had remained undisclosed for about 15 months. (The Chinese team published their findings , including the fatal case, in Cell on Oct. 26.) A founder of a rare-disease organization in China told me, on condition of anonymity for fear of political repercussions, that she had encountered other trials for genetic disorders in which deaths had gone unreported. Recent revelations of undisclosed deaths in clinical trials conducted in China have prompted warnings against the use of Chinese data in U.S. drug development.

As someone who has reported on China’s ethical governance for two decades, this all feels like déjà vu. Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies — that have earned the country a reputation as biotechnology’s “Wild East.”

Back in 2006, patients flocked to China to receive unproven stem-cell therapies . When immunotherapies came into vogue a decade later, bogus advertisements for unproven interventions proliferated online until the health ministry stepped in after the high-profile death of 21-year-old student Wei Zexi. Two years later, biophysicist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing the birth of the first genetically modified babies created using CRISPR technology.

The response in China to Mei’s death has been divided. Some netizens portray Qiu as a reckless scientist willing to gamble with patients’ lives. Others, including longtime acquaintances, describe him as a diligent scientist committed to helping patients. In some respects, Qiu represents the antithesis of He. After the CRISPR-babies scandal, Qiu openly condemned He’s reckless behavior — only to become embroiled in a comparable scandal himself six years later.

It might be tempting to blame such scandals on individual failings. The deeper questions are: What systemic factors shaped their behavior? What does the incident reveal about China’s Achilles heel in biotechnology—and about the broader culture of international science in which it is embedded? And what can the lessons teach clinical research worldwide?

Fatal Flaw

It would be unfair to suggest that China hasn’t tried to strengthen its ethical governance. The CRISPR-babies scandal prompted deep soul-searching among Chinese scholars and government officials. Since then, President Xi Jinping reportedly championed an “ethics first” approach, contrasting the “science first” mindset often seen in Chinese research. New measures have included incorporating ethics provisions in China’s first Civil Law Code, creating a national ethics committee , and enacting new ethics-review guidelines for clinical research.

But powerful forces are also pushing in the opposite direction. In 2016, China launched Healthy China 2030, making rapid application of emerging medical technologies in clinical practice a priority — not only to address unmet medical needs but to boost national competitiveness. Reforms created a new pathway to translate basic research into clinical applications for cutting-edge technologies overseen by the health ministry, alongside the conventional drug-approval route regulated by the National Medical Products Administration (NMPA), China’s equivalent of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This became widely known as the dual-track regulatory system.

“Since modern bioethics was introduced to China in the late 1980s, its history has been punctuated by one scandal after another — often fueled by hype surrounding emerging technologies.”

Under the technology track, clinical trials are often initiated by university researchers working with hospital clinicians rather than companies. Such investigator-initiated trials (IITs) exist worldwide. Until new regulations took effect this May, Chinese IITs were distinctive in that they could proceed with hospital approvals without the national regulatory oversight required for conventional drug trials. Compared with the NMPA route, the faster pathway allowed researchers to assess promising technologies in humans more quickly and at lower costs and help attract investment.

The result was a boom in IITs. By one estimate , more than 40,000 had been registered by April 2026, involving hundreds of thousands of participants and accounting for much of China’s translational research aimed at applying basic research to clinical practice.

China’s IIT model attracted worldwide attention. Kiran Musunuru, an expert on gene therapy at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia, told me that “there is a widespread perception” that Chinese-style IITs offer a way to conduct first-in-human trials quickly and inexpensively. U.S. companies are increasingly interested in conducting IITs in China. Some U.S. researchers have even argued that the U.S should adopt elements of China’s model to accelerate drug discovery and enhance its competitiveness.

Critics, however, point to a fatal flaw: quality control. Driven by the pursuit of high-impact papers— whether for career advancement or hospital rankings — researchers rushed into first-in-human trials of emerging technologies. Hospitals are overwhelmed by proposals involving technologies with varying levels of risk. Researchers told me that as many as two dozen applications can be assessed in a single afternoon. In many cases, the process has become “a rubber-stamping exercise,” explained Zhu Wei, a bioethicist at the Shanghai Clinical Research Center.

A recent analysis of Chinese stem-cell IITs found that although a small fraction helped accelerate the application of basic research to clinical practice, most were repetitive, lacked innovation and wasted resources. Musunuru — who led the landmark development of a personalized gene-editing trial for Baby KJ, an infant with a rare life-threatening deficiency of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase 1 that can cause dangerous ammonia buildup in the blood — warns that allowing individual hospitals to approve first-in-human trials of emerging technologies is particularly dangerous, because few researchers have sufficient experience to assess their risks. They would be “operating blind,” he told me, leaving the outcome dependent on “their appetite for risk.” That appetite can be amplified by institutional conflicts of interest. Successful trials of emerging technologies can bring researchers and hospitals fame, career advancement, high rankings and resources. Jing-Bao Nie, a bioethicist at the University of Otago in Dunedin, New Zealand, told me that these incentives can undermine institutional judgment and jeopardize patient safety. In Mei’s case, he noted, the lure of a “world-class breakthrough” may have overwhelmed necessary caution. Political interference, which is common in China, is another way the appetite for risk may outweigh caution. Chinese researchers told me that senior hospital leaders often chair the committees that review trial applications. When they seek to push through major projects led by prominent scientists, other committee members may feel unable to object. Read Noema in print. A central regulator is more insulated from such pressures and can also draw on a far broader pool of expertise. As Musumuru notes, the FDA has an army of experienced reviewers who have assessed successful and failed trials, as well as those involving serious adverse effects. Its decisions are therefore informed by “the widest possible body of knowledge,” he told me. “That’s very reassuring.” Oversight Deficiencies Zhai Xiaomei, a bioethicist at the Peking Union Medical College and a member of the national science and technology ethics committee, was not wrong when she told New Beijing News that the problems exposed by Mei’s tragedy had improved since China’s State Council Order No. 818, which established a new regulatory framework for clinical research and commercial application of cutting-edge biomedical technologies, took effect this May. Under the new rules, only top-tier hospitals can undertake IITs. Trials involving emerging technologies like gene and cell therapy, brain-machine interfaces, transplantation and microbial therapies must undergo further review by the health ministry after hospital approval. Adverse effects must be reported within five working days. Violations can result in fines, suspension or permanent ban on clinical research, loss of licenses and even criminal charges. The scientific community in China and abroad welcomes the new rules. But a researcher working closely with the ministry, who spoke on condition of anonymity due to potential career repercussions, told me that it lacks sufficient staff with the necessary technical expertise to review the large volume of applications. Consequently, the researcher added, the reviews rely heavily on experts from universities and hospitals, with only a handful assessing each case. By contrast, Musunuru told me that the U.S. FDA employs numerous in-house reviewers, many with decades of experience, and dozens pore over each submission. If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, he argues, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality. “If translating emerging technologies into clinical practice remains a national priority, China must make sustained investments in regulatory expertise to ensure trial safety and quality.” More troublingly, Order 818 lacks mechanisms to monitor what happens locally and identify violations. It includes neither an inspection process — a crucial component of regulatory oversight in countries such as the U.S. and UK — nor a whistleblowing platform for reporting adverse effects and deaths. Such mechanisms are particularly important in countries where transparency is limited, and the press is not free. Without them, violations may go unnoticed and the penalties risk becoming little more than empty threats. Researchers, like bioethicist Ma Yonghui of Xiamen University, also worry that regulatory exemptions could create loopholes. Military hospitals, for instance, fall outside health ministry rules. The two dozen or so free trade zones across China, particularly in Bo’ao on the tropical island of Hainan, may enjoy special regulatory treatment, potentially attracting foreign researchers and companies seeking to conduct ethically contentious trials they could not undertake in their own countries. There are ample precedents of scientists exploiting countries with weak ethics governance as sites for risky research. In October 2018, one month before the CRISPR-babies scandal, He and John Zhang, founder and medical director of the New Hope Fertility Center in New York City, met Hainan’s vice governor to discuss establishing a clinic in Bo’ao to offer experimental procedures, including heritable genome editing. Zhang had already attracted international attention in 2016 for helping produce in Mexico the world’s first “three-parent baby” to prevent the transmission of mitochondrial DNA mutations from the mother. The procedure involved replacing faulty mitochondria with healthy ones from a female donor during in vitro fertilization, a procedure that was — and still is — illegal in the U.S. Hype & Hope While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations, Nie told me. The case offers a window into people’s relationship with biotechnology in China as well as their hopes and expectations — shaped not only by scientists but by society at large. Over the past decade, rare-disease advocacy organizations have grown rapidly in China, helping improve patient care, pressing for government support and driving research through collecting genetic data, studying disease progression and funding clinical trials. Su Yeyang, an independent anthropologist in Langfang in Hebei province who works with rare-disease communities, told me this has given families a sense of agency. With limited social support and a market-driven drug-discovery model that has failed rare-disease communities worldwide, they are doing whatever they can “to help themselves, their children and their community,” she said. With gene therapy, the “magic cure” long hoped for by many rare-disease patients seems within reach. In one high-profile case, a fledgling company approached Xu Wei, a high-school graduate in his 30s in Kunming, in China’s southern province of Yunnan, to develop a gene therapy for his son. The boy had Menkes syndrome, a rare genetic disorder that impairs copper absorption and causes developmental delays and premature death. The company, with no track record in neurodevelopmental diseases, claimed to have developed the treatment in less than a year. In 2022, the 3-year-old received it at a private hospital in a trial that, based on publicly available accounts, appeared not to include biomarker or behavioral assessments of efficacy. Chinese media reported enthusiastically on anecdotal claims of improvements while downplaying the risks of undertaking such experimental therapies. A patient advocacy leader told me such cases are not uncommon in China, where at least 20 million people are living with rare diseases. They offer hope, whether grounded in evidence or not, and can encourage others to follow. “We try to explain to families that pouring millions into a trial is no guarantee of success” and could even backfire, she says. Even well-educated parents, like Mei’s, may underestimate the complexity of clinical research and overestimate what experimental therapies can achieve. It’s unclear whether Qiu, who was fired by the university last week and barred from participating in scientific research for five years following the government investigation , helped foster such expectations. He has not publicly given his account. But his book, “ The Autism Enlightenment ,” published this April, was revealing. It recounted how, in 2010, he told the mother of a child with Rett syndrome — a rare, genetic neurodevelopmental disorder leading to severe cognitive and physical impairments — that a cure would likely emerge in three to five years. It did not discuss fatal risks often associated with first-in-human trials. It did not mention Jessie Gelsinger, who had a mild form of ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency, a condition that can lead to abnormally high levels of ammonia in the blood and died in 1999 from a preventable complication of an experimental gene therapy. “While Mei’s death has prompted renewed soul-searching over China’s ethical failings, it would be a mistake to see it simply as a scientific scandal that can be fixed with new regulations.” Gelsinger was the first person publicly identified as having died in a gene therapy clinical trial, which undermined public trust in the field and set back its progress for decades. Nor did the book draw caution from the death in 2024 of a girl with Rett syndrome in the first brain-directed gene therapy for the condition. In both cases, scientists used the same type of virus as Qiu did. In a society where disability and genetic disease remain stigmatized, and families receive limited support, Mei’s parents placed their hopes in Qiu and gene editing. Like the couple who turned to He Jiankui to protect their children from HIV and the associated discrimination by editing their embryos, they sought a technological solution to social problems. As the Illness Challenge Foundation, a Beijing-based rare-disease advocacy organization, put it after Mei’s death , “responsible innovation should not entice patients to stake their lives in the name of hope.” China’s Gelsinger Moment? Gelsinger’s death in 1999 was a game changer. It’s widely regarded as a cautionary tale of how a toxic combination of scientific hype and insufficient safeguards can jeopardize patient safety. It triggered institutional reforms and significant changes in research culture in the U.S. that were aimed at rebuilding public and regulatory trust. Mei’s death could be China’s Gelsinger moment. It has exposed regulatory failings, a scientific ethos that encourages hype and recklessness, and deeper societal problems surrounding disability and genetic disease. None is unique to China, but they are particularly acute in a country facing a distinctive combination of political and developmental challenges. At the heart of the incident lies the “moral arbitrage” of experimental therapies, a recurrent theme in biotechnological innovation worldwide. On one hand, patients want access to cutting-edge, unproven treatments when they see them as their only hope. On the other hand, such treatments carry risks, which often accompany medical breakthroughs. Navigating the contours between hope and risk requires more than scientific evidence and regulatory rules, Su told me. It demands critical reflection on the culture of international science that places a premium on competition, sensational research, and being first at any cost. It also calls for broader societal dialogues about the diverse notions of human flourishing, the stigmatization of disabilities, and the need for greater support for people living with rare diseases. If China can learn from the failures and undertake the regulatory, scientific and social reforms needed to address its biotech governance failures — and if the rest of the world can look beyond the country’s small number of success stories out of a hidden ocean of low-quality and potentially harmful clinical trials — Mei’s death will not have been in vain. stories.body:
Warning: contains graphic content some readers may find upsetting

“Parts of my body were still wet, and when I looked around as I lay on the ground, I realised this was from the blood of my family,” he says. “Saynab’s head was severed from the rest of her body. My children were unrecognisable. Their bodies were very burned and black, ripped to pieces.”

Still, as he lost consciousness again, he was sure who they were. “I knew they were my daughters, because the body parts strewn out in the cave were so small.”

The spread of cheap drones means warfare is increasingly conducted by invisible armies at the push of a button. Victims have no warning and no chance for justice

Death had come from the sky for Mohamed’s family: an execution carried out with no warning, no trial, no guilty verdict or chance for recourse.

He did not even know who had carried out the killing, or under which authority – several nations have drones patrolling the skies of Somalia looking for Islamic State militants, including the US, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), Turkey and the Somali government. Any one of them could have pulled the trigger.

In Somalia, locals call these “ghost strikes” because the killer remains a phantom. With so many drones dropping bombs , and so many states (as well as non-state groups) operating their own drones, those being bombed may have little idea of who is killing them or precisely why.

Few countries publish data on where they carry out drone strikes, and even this is incomplete. Often, the only clues come from scattered fragments of bomb casings left behind, or what can be deduced from who is operating in the area or might have enemies there.

The phenomenon is a problem in countries far beyond Somalia. Ghost strikes reflect a fundamental shift in the way people conduct warfare. The machinery of war once required presence: soldiers on the ground or in the cockpit, tanks rolling through the streets, barracks and flags and bases. Only a small number of countries had the equipment – long-distance missiles and air forces – required to carry out a remote war, and those were relatively easy to monitor. Because most armies were physically present, there was also a stronger possibility of gathering evidence and holding them to account when it went terribly wrong: civilians massacred or war crimes committed.

Now, as cheap drones proliferate and become more accessible, thousands of civilians are being killed by remote control , at vast distances, sometimes by operators from countries with no boots on the ground at all. In Sudan’s brutal civil war, drones have rapidly overtaken ground troops as the leading cause of civilian death this year . Most often, no party takes responsibility for a strike. Last month, dozens of civilians were killed in strikes in Tigray, where Tigrayan, Ethiopian and Eritrean forces are all using drones – no one has claimed credit for the strikes or deaths.

On the Horn of Africa – which includes Somalia, Ethiopia and Sudan – the problem is playing out at a grand scale , with at least 11 nations or militant groups operating military drones in those three countries. But we are seeing the same thing in multiparty conflicts across the world, including Yemen, Iran, Myanmar and elsewhere.

According to new data from Drone Wars , more than 55 countries are now operating large, armed, predator-style drones, with seven other states due to acquire them soon. Chris Cole, director of Drone Wars, says this number is probably a significant undercount – the dataset doesn’t include the far cheaper one-way kamikaze models that detonate on impact, and there is nothing forcing countries or companies to announce when they have bought or sold drones, so many more could be acquiring them covertly.

Drones have also become stunningly cheap, in warfare terms. A US fighter jet costs between $80m (£66m) and $300m – amounts that once ensured air supremacy was the preserve of rich countries and centralised governments. But low-cost drones manufactured in Turkey and China are transforming the market, and creating a new set of drone superpowers. A Turkish-made medium altitude long endurance (Male) drone, which can conduct long-distance flights, is equipped with infrared cameras, stays airborne for more than 24 hours and carries more than about 130kg or 300lb of explosives, costs between $2m and $5m for each unit.

Since Turkey began introducing cheap predator-style military drones in the mid-2010s, followed by China in the 2020s, they have become new “drone superpowers” transforming the market and equipping dozens of new countries for air wars. Simpler drones, especially the kamikaze units, can now be bought for as little as $200, with hundreds of new drone startups entering the market, driven partly by the demand of the Russia-Ukraine war. The lower entry cost is shifting the balance of power in conflicts, inviting new players into air wars – even non-state actors including terrorist groups, militias and drug cartels are increasingly acquiring armed drones. It is also making it far harder to track who is killing who.

“The more they proliferate, the more state and non-state actors lay their hands on these cheap drones, the more it makes accountability then really, really difficult,” says Abdullahi Halakhe, an expert on security in the Horn of Africa and Great Lakes region. “This is now one of the biggest problems for civilian protection.”

For Mohamed to learn who had killed his family on 21 May, it would require identifying the bomb fragments, tracing them back to the country of manufacture and finding out who had bought them.

First, however, he had to survive.

Mobile reception is limited in the Golis mountains, and he knew the nearest mobile phone mast was 3 miles (5km) away. The only way to find help was to drag himself in that direction.

It was about noon when Abdullahi Omar, a resident in the nearby coastal town of Buruc, received a phone call saying something had happened in the mountains. The call came in from a nomad outside Baxaya who had come across Mohamed, terribly injured, at a river not far from the cave.

Immediately, Omar began organising a team of men to go out and investigate. “We prepared 36 men in town to go out to Baxaya,” he says.

double quotation mark Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.

The group of men trekked about 19 miles, leaving Buruc during afternoon prayers and walking through the night to reach the site of the strike the following morning. Among those who volunteered for the long hike through the mountains was Mohamed Hassan. “When we finally made it to Baxaya we came across the dead family and injured man,” he says. “There were no Daesh [Islamic State] fighters anywhere, only the bodies of women and children.”

The Golis mountains have been the centre of a global war against the Islamic State in Somalia, with the US carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in the region . The UAE has carried out strikes in the area, but does not publish any data on how many. And Turkey and Somalia’s governments are both also using Bayraktar drones for strikes in Somalia, but publish such minimal data that it is difficult to confirm exactly when or where.

Baxaya, where Mohamed and his family were hit, was supposedly designated a “safe zone” by the Puntland regional government – which was confirmed by Somalia’s deputy ambassador to Tanzania, Ashkir Nuur, who represents the constituency.

“The Puntland authorities have not apologised nor compensated the sole survivor. It happened under their jurisdiction but the sole survivor is yet to receive answers,” Nuur says.

Local people say there were no Islamic State fighters nearby, and Male drone systems are equipped with sensitive, infrared camera systems for monitoring targets that should make it easy to distinguish a fighting force from a family with young children and 250 goats. Who, then, carried out the strike?

The men gathered up the pieces of Mohamed’s children, wrapping them in cloth for burial. As they worked, they heard the insect moan of drones above.

“While collecting the body parts of the family members, we could hear loud engines of planes – we couldn’t see them but could hear,” Hassan says. “Everyone who was picking up the body parts and wrapping up the remains had the sense that the same planes who massacred this family were now watching us.”

The men worked as quickly as they could. They took a series of photos and videos to document the strike’s aftermath, showing the bodies of Seynab, Fadumo, Aman and Anab, and the strewn bodies of dead goats. Photographs and video of the strike site taken by these first responders and reviewed by the Guardian confirm Mohamed’s description of events, including the catastrophic blast injuries to his wife, her unborn child, their three daughters, and the subsequent explosion that killed hundreds of his goats. The Guardian is not publishing these images due to their graphic nature.

In a video from the scene, one man stands before the four wrapped bodies, after they have been prepared for burial, and says: “The missile massacred the people right here, and as you have been told, these are their bodies. We want the world to watch this and know.”

Among the drying blood and debris, the men found something else: the shattered pieces of two missile casings, lying in the dirt. With no country claiming responsibility for the strike on the family, these dusty chunks of metal would provide the only evidence trail between the family who died, their killers and the booming, multibillion-dollar industry that provided the equipment.

Independent munitions experts Trevor Ball and NR Jenzen-Jones, of Armament Research services, have analysed the images of bomb fragments left at the scene for the Guardian and concluded that they are from a MAM-series munition, manufactured by the Turkish state-owned defence manufacturer Roketsan.

Jenzen-Jones says the “bomb remnants pictured probably evidence a strike by an unmanned aerial vehicle [UAV], mostly likely a Bayraktar TB2”.

The drone is named for its creator – Selçuk Bayraktar, one of the stars of Turkey’s drone industry. His company, Baykar, has had a meteoric rise since it brought the first Bayraktar drone on to the global market in 2014, and works closely with state-owned defence companies, arming its drones with Rokestan munitions. In 2016, Bayraktar married Sümeyye Erdoğan, the daughter of the president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, in a lavish wedding ceremony, drawing Baykar into even closer connection with its government.

Turkey is a relatively recent entrant to the drone market, but it has rapidly dominated sales to new states buying large, predator-style drones – particularly across African and Arab countries. On the back of its drone manufacturers, the country’s entire defence export market has boomed, reaching more than £7.5bn last year , up more than 500% from a decade earlier . The country now claims to control 65% of the global drone market , and Baykar has become one of the world’s biggest military drone companies. This year, the country’s military exports are tracking toward a new record high.

At the same time, Turkey has developed a reputation for relatively lax “no questions asked” export rules. A large portion of the governments that Turkey has sold drones to in the past five years are classed as fully authoritarian regimes (including Mali, Azerbaijan, Kyrgyzstan, Rwanda, Turkmenistan, Qatar, Uzbekistan, Chad, Togo, Niger, Tunisia, Djibouti, Burkina Faso, Kuwait, Libya, Somalia) and/or already embroiled in civil war or armed internal conflict (including but not limited to Sudan, Ethiopia, Nigeria, Somalia) . Numerous states on Turkey’s customer list have subsequently been accused of mass killings of civilians using their equipment. For Ankara, however, the explosion of the drone market has been a geopolitical success – with Turkey leveraging drone sales to massively grow its overseas political and military influence.

A Turkish diplomatic representative said: “Turkish UAV exports to Sudan or Somalia, like those to other countries, are subject to guarantees that they will be used in full compliance with international law. There is no verified information indicating that Turkish-manufactured UAVs have been used in violation of the relevant international norms and regulations by the Sudanese Army or in Somalia.”

Even tracing the missile that killed Mohamed’s family to its source, however, does not tell us who was responsible for pulling the trigger. The UAE, Turkey and the Somali government all fly Bayraktar drones in Somali skies. The US has also carried out hundreds of strikes in the region, but using its own drones.

The Turkish, Somali and UAE governments did not respond to requests for comment on who dropped the bomb on Mohamed and his family. Here, the trail runs cold. Seynab, Aman, Anab and Fadumo’s killers remain ghosts.

Hours after they arrived, the men began the long trek back through the mountains toward the coast. Hassan was one of those who carried Mohamed, hauling his body over the difficult, rocky terrain of the mountains for more than 24 hours.

The whole way, the sound of planes followed them.

“It would go away, then once again the noise would return, so we knew our every step was being watched,” Hassan says. “We were scared because we knew what the planes did to Mohamed and his family … They were innocent people, who did nothing wrong and were massacred by these same planes now hovering above us.” From Buruc, the company sent Mohamed on a raft to Bosaso, the nearest equipped hospital, for treatment.

Before Mohamed had even arrived at the hospital, Abdulkadir Koudah, a family member, had heard the news and contacted local security services to inform them that a man who was the sole survivor of an airstrike was on his way. In the months since, “they haven’t helped us or given us any answers on who bombed the family”, he says.

Mohamed is slowly recovering, although the wounds are still visible on his body. Still, he says: “The burns on my body are nothing compared to what my daughters went through.

“They were excited about having another sibling and so was their mother, but everything changed in the blink of an eye and I don’t know who to blame.”

stories.title: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia is elite impunity | Moira Donegan
stories.summary: After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people There are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time. But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration, Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist Continue reading...
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
After the CEO was reinstated after Trump’s pressure campaign, it is abundantly clear: there are different rules for rich people

T here are different rules for rich people. If you or I acted the way that Jensen Huang has been accused of acting – allegedly berating and mistreating employees, sleeping with subordinates, and seeming to carry on a staggering number of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman identified by US intelligence as a likely Chinese spy who helped smuggle the company’s product to China – we probably would find ourselves out of work and out of favor for quite some time.

But this is not so for Huang, the tech founder and close ally to Donald Trump who was recently ousted from Nvidia, the chip manufacturer he founded. On Monday, after a pressure campaign from Donald Trump, JD Vance and other members of the Trump administration , Huang was reinstated as CEO by the Nvidia board.

His alleged actions had risked national security; his fall from power lasted less than two weeks.

According to early reporting, Trump decided late last week to intervene in Huang’s case, thinking that his restoration as Nvidia’s chief could help rally a sluggish stock market. In an economy that has become increasingly dependent on the success of AI companies, Nvidia , which makes the chips that enable the technology, has come to be seen as something of a load-bearing firm, propping up an AI sector which is increasingly understood to be in an overvaluation bubble that will inevitably pop.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a Truth Social post. The reinstatement was reportedly orchestrated by Vance, the vice-president and presumptive 2028 Republican nominee, who drew on his own deep ties to friends, allies and benefactors in Silicon Valley to convey the administration’s strong desire for Huang to return.

It marks a remarkable intervention of the executive branch into the personnel decisions of a private firm.

In public statements, Huang’s allies and boosters have repeatedly emphasized the restored CEO as personally essential to the company, downplaying the national security and chip-smuggling concerns in favor of a portrait of a singular mind.

Huang, they say, is unique and irreplaceable, essential to the functioning of Nvidia and hence of the economy; because of this supposed personal specialness, we’re told, it makes sense if he got to spill secrets to China over pillow talk at the expense of your retirement fund.

But it is striking that this deep belief in the irreplaceable brilliance of one AI CEO is so profoundly at odds with the ethos of the AI industry, which promises to automate away all human judgment and experience and make human beings in general – let along any one human being in particular – profoundly replaceable, if not completely superfluous.

Maybe this, too, is another way that the rules are different for the rich: the tech executives never meant to say that they themselves would become disposable and interchangeable. That fate was reserved for the lowly, like you and me.

It is just this sort of shocking arrogance and display of elite impunity among the tech sector that has disgusted Americans and shocked their consciences; the deep and emphatic rejection of datacenters that was expressed by voters in the recent midterm elections should be understood, I think, as a proxy for a bigger discontent with the recklessness and greed of the tech oligarchs who impose their whims on the country with life-altering consequences.

It is not clear, either, why the Trump administration, which claims that national security and the US economy rely on the returns of AI companies, would want one of the most important of those companies to be helmed by a man who may have been compromised by China, the nation’s primary adversary and main economic competitor.

The flagrancy of the seeming corruption and incompetence at play, and the evident rage of the American people at both, will hopefully spur Democrats to launch serious and probing investigations into Nvidia, Huang and their ties to the Trump administration when the party takes control of both houses of Congress in January.

In the meantime, Trump himself has indicated that there’s one reason why he has taken a particular interest in Huang’s case: sex. In a statement to the Times, Trump said that he thought Huang had been treated unfairly because of the sexual nature of his scandal, or what the president called “The Peyton Place part” – an evident reference, the Times helpfully explained to its less senior readers, to a 1960s soap opera that featured many sex scandals.

“Without that, it would have been a lot easier,” Trump said, “because that got the attention. You know, sex was involved, and sex sells better than stocks.” Call it a kind of sex-pest solidarity. The president, a habitual adulterer who has been accused of sexual misconduct by more than two dozen women and who paid an adult film star to keep quiet about their alleged affair (all of which he denies), seems to see something of himself in the prolifically and allegedly perhaps treasonably adulterous Jensen Huang. Elite impunity may have extra appeal when it can double as male impunity, too.

As if to emphasize the point, Trump took to Truth Social to share an AI-generated image of Jensen Huang, in a pose mimicking a famous photograph of Trump himself rising up in the moments after an assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania, in the summer of 2024. In the original photo, Trump held up a fist in triumph, showing that he had survived the gunman’s shots. In the new version that the president posted on Monday morning, Huang held up a red bra.

stories.body:
China-made lithium-ion batteries, which are relatively low-cost, dominate Ofgem project shortlist

A string of battery projects linked to China are expected to be granted UK state subsidies despite deepening fears over the risk of foreign interference they could pose to Europe’s energy systems.

Ofgem, Great Britain’s energy regulator, published a provisional shortlist for a new “long duration” energy storage scheme in June. The list was dominated by projects relying on lithium-ion batteries, which are typically manufactured in China and operated with Chinese software.

The low cost of lithium-ion batteries meant 11 projects were able to outcompete homegrown renewable energy storage technologies to make Ofgem’s 16-strong shortlist in line for financial support. The energy watchdog is expected to confirm the final projects selected for financial support in the coming weeks.

The shortlisted projects include some backed by developers that routinely rely on Chinese battery makers, one of which was recently the subject of an “ethical hack” by a German cybersecurity company that claimed to have accessed hundreds of thousands of solar installations across Europe.

Ofgem is under pressure to bring forward investment in battery projects that can store renewable energy and release it back to the grid for at least eight – hours at a time to help reduce the cost of balancing the grid.

But senior industry sources have said that the regulator’s assessment criteria for its new battery support scheme have not adequately considered the security and economic benefits of backing British storage technologies over cheaper Chinese imports.

Invinity Energy Systems, a British producer of vanadium flow batteries , threatened to reconsider its plans to manufacture batteries in the UK after Ofgem selected just one project that uses its alternative energy storage technology in its shortlist.

The regulator is expected to finalise the scheme months after a report by Michael Collins, a former deputy head of national security strategy at the UK Cabinet Office, warned that Europe was “sleepwalking” into a series of economic and national security problems because of an overreliance on Chinese-made green technology.

Ofgem’s assessment is heavily weighted towards the cost of each project. Although the regulator considers each project’s proposed IT and security measures, this is based on the extent to which these systems might delay “their stated delivery timelines” in the early 2030s.

The regulator does not appear to specifically consider the risk of security breaches during the lifetime of the projects once they are delivered, although developers would be expected to comply with the government’s general cybersecurity guidance.

A spokesperson for Ofgem said: “We assessed projects against the legal and policy framework set by government and parliament, and are carefully considering consultation responses before reaching final decisions.”

Battery developers Field Energy and Statera Energy, which are behind seven of the lithium-ion projects shortlisted by Ofgem, both have long-established links to Chinese manufacturers which provided the batteries used in past projects.

after newsletter promotion

Field Energy is behind five projects on the shortlist and has typically sourced its battery technology from Envision Energy, one of six companies closely linked to the Chinese Communist party according to US senators.

Statera had three projects shortlisted, including one pumped hydro power project and two lithium-ion batteries, and in the past sourced batteries from Envision, as well as the Chinese solar and battery maker Sungrow. Sungrow was the company targeted in the ethical hack earlier this year.

Both companies said they took security seriously and complied with all national security guidance at their sites. Amit Gudka, the chief executive of Field and the former boss of collapsed energy supplier Bulb , said the company wanted to play a part in creating a UK-based battery manufacturing industry to support future projects.

A UK government spokesperson said: “The security of our energy system is our priority and we are taking action to build secure and resilient battery supply chains and reduce vulnerabilities, while investment in the UK’s energy sector is subject to the highest levels of national security scrutiny.”
