stories.body:
Anthony Albanese and Matthew Wale sign new treaty as Solomon Islands PM states his country no longer ‘a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region’

The Solomon Islands prime minister says the days of his country being an uncertain partner in the Pacific are over as he signed a sweeping agreement to make Australia his country’s primary security partner and limit ties with China.

Matthew Wale signed the new treaty with Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese , in Canberra on Wednesday after Solomon Islands earlier this week announced it was terminating a landmark security pact with Beijing.

The deal includes $740m in new funding from Australia over 10 years, comprising $670m in grants and $70m in loans. Money is expected to flow from January.

The treaty is a blow to China’s efforts to build influence with Pacific Island nations and a major win for the Albanese government’s campaign to rebuild ties across the region. A backlash is expected from Beijing, which has used missile tests and military exercises to express its displeasure in the past.

“Solomon Islands has been, for a number of years, a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region,” Wale said. “Those days are done. Gone. We don’t want to be there again.”

The deal means Solomon Islands will not allow foreign military bases or major security infrastructure to be developed on its territory. Sensitive systems will remain “free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access”.

Chinese police officers are expected to leave Solomon Islands by the middle of 2027. About 14 officers have been posted to the country under the expiring deal with Beijing.

Honiara has secured new funding from Australia for policing services and improved visa arrangements, allowing Solomon Islands citizens to stay in Australia for longer periods. An expansion of the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme is planned to allow Solomons citizens to work in early childhood education and aged care.

Australia’s funding will help provide universal access to education, from kindergarten to year 12. A third of Solomon Islands children do not attend school and less than 20% complete year 12.

Australia and Solomon Islands have agreed to advance joint economic, development and security priorities through the deal, with Australia pledging to invest in community development, education and infrastructure.

Australia will also increase funding for the Solomon Kings football club, including player development.

“This treaty will strengthen our security partnership,” Albanese said.

“Australia is proud to be Solomon Islands’ main security partner, and that’s a responsibility that we take seriously. We’ll continue working with Solomon Islands to keep its community safe, to strengthen its police force and improve border security.

“We’ll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions.”

after newsletter promotion

Wale said secrecy provisions prevented him from speaking publicly when asked about ending the pact with Beijing. The five-year deal was due to expire in April and will not be renewed.

“We have ongoing discussions with China, but of course today is about our relationship with Australia and the treaty that we’ve signed,” he said.

Albanese welcomed more than 15 Solomon Island cabinet ministers as part of the official delegation visiting Canberra. Their presence and Wale’s confidence at surviving any fresh no confidence motions in parliament signalled the stronger relationship could last.

Albanese and senior Australian ministers including Penny Wong, Pat Conroy and Richard Marles stepped up engagement in the Pacific after Labor’s election win in 2022. Labor has signed new alliances and agreements with countries including Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Fiji.

The Coalition could oppose the new treaty because of language about a transition to net zero carbon emissions by 2050. Earlier this week, the opposition said it would not support Australia’s Nakamal agreement with Vanuatu on similar grounds. It said future governments should not be bound to energy policy settings because of foreign treaties.

Asked about the termination of the Solomon Islands deal, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said on Tuesday that no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation existed in Beijing’s cooperation with the Pacific.

“China always follows the principle of mutual respect and equality in developing relations with the Solomon Islands.

“Our cooperation does not target any third party and is not subject to third-party influence.”

China’s embassy in Canberra was contacted for comment.

stories.body:
Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025

China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.

China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.

The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.

Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged .

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.

He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.

The hashtag “Chen Jining under investigation” had amassed about 240m views on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo by Wednesday morning, with many users saying they were “shocked” and “stunned” in comments under state media posts.

“This is arguably the biggest political news to come out of China in a few years,” Taisu Zhang, a professor at Yale Law School specialising in contemporary Chinese law and politics, wrote on X.

Zhang pointed to Chen’s status as a rising political star who had been seen as “a near-lock for the politburo Standing Committee”, China’s highest political decision-making body.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign , which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged , including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.

“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ‘self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.

“If anything, it continues to intensify.”

The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.

Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

“Chen Jining is no ordinary fallen official … [He is] an exemplar of someone who rose from the specialised field of environmental protection to the pinnacle of political power,” Mao Shoulong, a professor of public administration and policy at Renmin University of China, wrote in a commentary on WeChat.

“His downfall, therefore, is not merely that of an individual, but of an entire type of official, a model of political advancement, and a set of assumptions about the relationship between technology and politics, expertise and power, and competence and loyalty,” Mao wrote.

Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.

stories.title: MP calls for action after her likeness used for AI porn deepfakes
stories.summary: Mims Davies urged people to report any incidents so that “culprits can be held to account”.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Davies said she was concerned similar incidents could put women off entering politics

Published 5 hours ago

A member of parliament whose name and image were used in AI content on porn sites said the issue could make women less likely to want to enter public life.

Mims Davies, the shadow Welsh Secretary, said she received an email in her parliamentary inbox which said "her likeness was found on forums in abusive and pornographic content".

The Conservative frontbencher said people making money from deepfakes was "grotesque", urging people to report it if it happens to them so that "culprits can be held to account".

"It's completely unacceptable, it's a violation and an outrage," she told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast .

Deepfakes are videos, pictures or audio clips made with artificial intelligence to look real .

It is illegal , external to share or threaten to share intimate photos or videos of someone without their consent, including through deepfake images.

Davies said she had waived her right to anonymity to call for more resources to find and prosecute culprits.

Ofcom, the communications regulator, said "significant action is being taken to tackle intimate image abuse" but added there was "more to do".

Davies, MP for East Grinstead and Uckfield in East Sussex, said: "There are things you expect to be dealing with these days in public life and frankly this is not it.

"This could be any woman. This could be anyone in politics, in business, or down in your high street.

"We need to be able to protect ourselves from deepfakes."

She added: "This is going to have an effect on our daily lives, on our lifestyles. We need an answer to this.

"There's a problem, a new frontier which we need to battle."

She previously told the BBC she was spiked on a night out in 2019.

Mims Davies: My likeness was found in abusive and pornographic content

24 November 2026

Shadow Welsh Secretary Mims Davies says her name and image were used on porn sites without her consent, and warns it's putting women off entering politics.

Davies, who studied politics and international relations at Swansea University before embarking on a career in journalism in Wales, said the issue was likely to make women "feel less likely to want to enter public life".

"It doesn't just affect you personally, it affects families. You never know when you're walking into a room what people might be thinking.

"We need more women in public life at every single level, from councillors, to Westminster and to the Senedd. It's tough out there.

"We need those kinds of voices in the room."

Her office confirmed reports have been made to the Metropolitan Police and parliamentary authorities.

Davies called for more resources to find and prosecute culprits

An Ofcom spokesperson said: "Nobody should have to experience the trauma of having an explicit deepfake created or shared without their consent.

"Under the Online Safety Act, tech firms must assess and mitigate the risk of UK users encountering illegal content like this on their sites and apps, and remove it quickly when they become aware of it.

"We've laid down clear expectations for how platforms should do this – including by using automated technology to deal with illegal intimate images – and we've driven some of the strongest changes of any online safety regulation in the world.

"We've also shown we'll take action if evidence suggests companies are falling short."

In January, Ofcom launched an investigation into X over concerns its AI tool Grok was being used to create sexualised images.

The regulator gave platforms until the end of September this year to take effective steps to stop illegal intimate images and deepfakes from spreading.

At the time, it warned that any firms which breached their duties would face fines of up to 10% of their global annual revenue.

The Department for Culture, Media and Sport has been approached for comment.

Watch: Badenoch presses PM over university fees for EU students

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has challenged Andy Burnham over whether EU students in the UK could pay lower university tuition fees as part of his deal with the bloc.

The prime minister insisted the issue of tuition fees was "a separate deal", with discussions on this continuing.

Asked whether he could rule out EU students paying the same fees as British students, Burnham said this was "the European negotiating position" and "won't be put on the table".

At a UK-EU summit last Friday, the two sides agreed a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth travel scheme .

A joint statement said they would also work towards a "supplementing" agreement on tuition fees for EU students in the UK and British students in the EU, with negotiations concluding within six months.

EU sources had earlier suggested the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

But the UK has insisted the wider deal will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can reach an agreement on tuition fees.

Deal with EU not dependent on tuition fees agreement, Miliband says Published 4 days ago

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start? Published 5 days ago

At the moment, EU students at UK universities generally pay the same fees as international students, ranging from £11,400 to £38,000.

For British undergraduate students tuition fees are currently capped at £9,790 a year.

Universities have raised concerns that capping EU student fees at the same level could cost hundreds of millions a year, at a time when the sector is struggling financially.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch asked Burnham who would pick up the bill if EU and British students paid the same fees, "cash-strapped universities or cash-strapped taxpayers?"

In response, the PM said "the deal on tuition fees is not done", adding: "We will take that conversation forward always rightfully mindful of the challenges faced by higher education."

Pressed over whether the EU would still sign his wider deal if he refused to cut fees for European students, Burnham said legislation introduced in Parliament on Thursday would set a date for the implementation of deals on food, emissions and a youth experience scheme.

He added: "We will continue discussions with the European Union on the question of tuition fees."

Asked if he would rule out EU students paying the same tuition fees as British students, Burnham replied: "She is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position.

"That has not been put on the table. It won't be put on the table."

Asked if Burnham was saying EU students would not pay domestic fees, the prime minister minister's official spokesman told reporters he would not get ahead of the outcome of ongoing talks.

stories.title: EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme
stories.summary: The draft proposal could see the UK join the scheme without having to increase import taxes on Chinese cars.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 November 2026

The UK could be included in the EU's proposed scheme to protect car manufacturing in Europe without Britain having to impose import taxes on Chinese electric cars, under draft plans.

The proposal has been drawn up by Ireland, which currently holds the EU's rotating presidency, and will be discussed by EU governments.

It comes after previous suggestions the EU would demand the UK align its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles as a condition of joining the scheme.

Senior figures in the British government have been talking increasingly positively about the potential to join on terms London would be willing to sign up to, and are cautiously optimistic about this latest move.

The "Made in Europe" scheme, known formally as the Industrial Accelerator Act, aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries, with a particular focus on both China and the car industry.

The idea is potentially dangerous to the UK, as being outside the EU would mean being exposed to restrictions principally intended for others.

Germany and France had previously agreed a joint position under which UK involvement would have been conditional on matching EU import restrictions and tariffs on imports of Chinese electric cars and hybrids.

Alignment in this area with the EU would increase the price of increasingly popular Chinese cars in the UK, as well as raising the prospect of a potential Chinese retaliation with its own tariffs imposed on British-made cars.

'Real concern'

Now Ireland, as first reported by the Financial Times , external , is suggesting the UK could join Made in Europe without the need to match the EU's tariffs.

The argument made in favour of this is the UK and EU car industries are so heavily integrated and interdependent.

The proposal, which would also apply to Switzerland and countries in the European Economic Area (EEA) such as Norway, would depend on the non-EU countries granting the EU access to their subsidy and procurement schemes.

However, the idea is still at its early stages. It will first be discussed by EU ambassadors, before it is considered by competition ministers from the EU's member states at a meeting next month.

The proposal would also have to be accepted by the European Commission and the European Parliament.

Andy Burnham has previously pushed for UK inclusion in the scheme to avoid "collateral damage" to British industry.

Speaking at Prime Minister's Questions on Wednesday, he claimed the government had successfully "removed the threat" from the Made in Europe scheme as part of talks over the EU deals he agreed last week .

Pressed later whether he had overstated how advanced talks were on the EU side, the prime minister's spokesman said: "We continue to engage on these issues with Europe in a genuine spirit of cooperation."

A spokesperson for the Irish presidency said it had proposed a "pragmatic and balanced way forward" on the scheme, having "listened closely to all member states".

stories.title: No 10 does not rule out inviting back influencer at centre of video row
stories.summary: It comes after Kemi Badenoch called on the PM to apologise for allowing an "obscene" video to be recorded outside Number 10.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 25 November 2026

Downing Street has not ruled out inviting the creator of a video which was branded "not acceptable" by Andy Burnham to future events at Number 10.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on the PM to apologise for "debasing his office" by allowing Max Balegde to record a video on the steps of Number 10, which included "vile" and "obscene" comments about women.

Burnham said the video had been taken down and Balegde had "rightly apologised" for it - but he said he would not apologise for engaging with influencers who could reach young people.

Asked repeatedly whether Balegde would be invited back, the prime minister's official spokesman said: "I'm not going to get ahead of future events."

Max Balegde has 3.6m followers on TikTok and 640,000 on Instagram

The spokesman was responding to a comment the influencer filmed after he had left the event on 9 November and posted in a YouTube video before the public criticism.

In it, Max Balegde said of the event the PM hosted, "well guys that was a huge success, Andy's invited me round for tea".

The PM's spokesman was unable to confirm whether that invite was legitimate or whether a further meeting would go ahead.

Downing Street also could not say whether Balegde had ever been paid taxpayer money to collaborate with the government on social media posts.

No influencers were paid to attend the Downing Street reception, the PM's spokesman added, but influencers have in the past been paid when working with other government departments.

About 60 content creators were invited to the Downing Street reception on 9 November, with videos from the event, including of Burnham DJing, subsequently emerging online.

In one video, Max Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, mouths the words "bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets", using audio from a meme that is trending online.

At Prime Minister's Questions, Badenoch said the words used were "so offensive that I will not repeat them in this House".

"Disgusting and pejorative comments about women's private parts, obscene language that referred to white women as cheap meat.

"This is grotesque. Labour MPs constantly tell us about their commitment to fighting violence against women and girls. Those MPs were silent yesterday, I won't be."

Burnham said the Tory leader was "right to call out that, because it was not acceptable" but he would "not apologise" for engaging with young people.

"She sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers," he added, accusing Badenoch of "having nothing positive to say to the country" and of "constantly talking it down".

The two leaders continued the argument throughout their weekly Commons clash, with Burnham saying "it's true I have spoken to influencers, and then I have to come to this House, with the opposite of influencers".

Badenoch said the PM preferred to "take questions to people dancing around Downing Street", a reference to a video of another content creator dancing through Number 10 and down the stairs in an attempt to recreate a scene from the film Love, Actually.

This prompted Burnham to make a jibe about "lockdown parties" in Downing Street during the Covid pandemic.

Responding to the row about his now-deleted TikTok video in an Instagram post on Tuesday, Balegde said: "My content is always meant to be silly, fun, and light-hearted.

"If anybody was offended by that video, I sincerely apologise."

But he said "nobody was offended for weeks until revolting right-wing people tried to put this disgusting narrative on it".

"And if anybody then looks at the video and is offended, I get that. So hence why I took it down because I think that is disgusting."

Sophie Tea, from the West Midlands, now lives and works in London

Videos which were filmed inside the Downing Street premises were recorded on government phones.

Attendees at the event have confirmed they had to hand personal devices in and were given a phone and a camera to film with, with the footage they recorded sent to them after the event.

Artist Sophie Tea, who has more than 1.3 million followers on TikTok, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been "excited" to be invited to the Downing Street reception, describing it as a "privilege".

"I believe in the democratization of information and I think this opportunity was perfect for me to be able to understand more what's going on.

"Number 10 is meant to represent the whole country and the more people feel like they belong there, the better."

She said she was looking to use her social media platform to "communicate to the UK some of the brilliant things that are happening in government".

Asked if she was being used by the government, she said "absolutely" but it was "mutually exploitative" because, as an independent artist, she had used it to "prop up my own value".

Tories accuse Burnham of turning No 10 into 'joke' after influencer video row Published 1 day ago

Artist among first to sell work on TikTok Shop Published 29 March

This isn't the first time influencers have been invited into Downing Street. Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak was interviewed by content creators during his time in office.

Nor is it the first time they have descended onto Number 10 en masse, with the first content creator reception taking place under Sir Keir Starmer's leadership in 2025.

Content creators are also regularly invited to press conferences and government briefings, including an event at Number 11 Downing Street on the day of the Budget last month.

Writing on X, Luke Tryl, the UK director of pollsters More In Common, said it was "sensible" for Burnham to use influencers to reach a wider audience and it was "helping the PM seem in touch".

But, he added, the PM's "biggest weakness" was being seen as a "people pleaser" and he should also do "non-softball interviews with traditional scrutiny media" to help tackle that.

stories.title: Nuclear test veterans will get full truth, says Burnham, as he confirms independent panel
stories.summary: The prime minister says a Hillsborough-style independent panel will examine the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

stories.body:

Watch: 'The truth will have its own power,' Burnham says

Published 24 November 2026

Andy Burnham has told nuclear test veterans they will get "the full truth" as he confirmed plans for an investigation into the health legacy of Britain's Cold War-era atomic programme.

The prime minister has ordered an independent panel to assess the potential impact of testing exercises in the 1950s and 1960s.

Burnham told veterans and their families that the government would treat the process with the "utmost seriousness", later telling the Commons an interim report would be published by the 75th anniversary of the first test, in October next year.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) has for decades denied it covered up the impact of radiation on troops ordered to carry out nuclear weapons tests.

A BBC Newsnight special programme heard reaction from veterans, including John Morris, a laundry operator at a nuclear test site who went on to develop cancer and lost a four-month-old son. He believes both were linked to radiation exposure.

He said: "Seventy-two years ago I was an 18-year-old, sent to Christmas Island, totally unaware of what I was being led into.

"I am here today and I am looking for, and sincerely hope we will get, justice."

BBC Newsnight special on nuclear test veterans

Victoria Derbyshire speaks to veterans as an independent panel is announced into health impacts

Watch now on iPlayer

Veterans who were involved in the tests, predominantly carried out in Australia and the South Pacific, have long called for a full investigation into the long-term health effects it had on them and their children.

Many of the surviving veterans say they were more likely to develop a range of illnesses in the years that followed, while their descendants say they have suffered an increased risk of hereditary illnesses and fertility problems.

Veterans have recounted being ordered to fly through radioactive clouds without protection, witnessing atomic explosions with nothing to shield them from the fallout, and living on sand they believe was contaminated with nuclear material.

The announcement of an independent panel is the culmination of years of campaigning by the Labrats (Legacy of the Atomic Bomb: Recognition for Atomic Test Survivors) group and others, and comes 14 years after a legal challenge at the UK Supreme Court failed.

Many veterans have died in the decades since the tests, but some of those still alive shared their stories with Newsnight on Tuesday.

Brian Unthank says he witnessed three hydrogen bomb explosions in the Pacific without protective equipment and went to on develop multiple skin cancers.

He said: "I've always wanted to get a prime minister... to stand up in Parliament and make a total, abject apology for the total mess-up of the way they treated us veterans and the families through this 74 years.

"Next year is our 75th year of misery. Let's get it done today."

To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Watch: Nuclear test veterans speak to BBC about search for justice

Barbara Quick, whose father served in the RAF Police on Christmas Island - a major site for UK and US nuclear testing in the Pacific Ocean - told BBC Newsnight she had never been able to have children and two of her sister's children had died. She blames health complications arising from their father's exposure to radiation.

She said: "If you were higher personnel you got the gas mask, you got the suit - but my father was told to turn his collar up, turn his back and cover his eyes."

Steve Purse, whose father was a nuclear test veteran, was born with complex disabilities he says have never been fully diagnosed. He told BBC Newsnight the announcement was "huge" but that the panel must be allowed to provide full disclosure.

He said: "No-one has listened to us like this before, it's a moment of history."

Before becoming prime minister earlier this year, Burnham told BBC Newsnight the nuclear veterans had been subjected to a "criminal cover-up on an industrial scale" and backed calls for an investigation.

On Tuesday, he told campaigners at Downing Street: "All I can say is you know the courage you've shown, the dignity you've shown through the whole thing, given everything that happened, is honestly something that we just are in awe of.

"Your patience, your strength, your determination - and we will make sure that this process moves as quickly as possible to get you what you long deserved, which is the full truth... Obviously, I do not know what the full truth will be, but we will get it."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told campaigners in Downing Street that he would launch an independent investigation

Alan Owen, whose father was exposed to radiation while serving with the Royal Navy and died aged 52, told BBC Breakfast that along with the inquiry other measures had also been agreed, including a new education programme about nuclear test veterans and research for descendants who believe their conditions may be linked to the radiation tests.

"It's going to take time, but it needs to be done correctly," he said.

The prime minister told the Commons on Wednesday that an interim report would be followed by final findings "as quickly as possible".

Burnham said further action on education and research will continue while work on the report is being done, including organising a national memorial service for next October, on the 75th anniversary of the first test.

Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was "absolutely right" to talk about justice for veterans, but asked whether the government had made provisions for issuing compensation if necessary.

The prime minister said: "We should go wherever the truth takes us and we should make whatever recompense is needed as a result but those are questions that will come in the next phase."

The MoD has previously said four studies found no increased health risks for those involved with the tests, as did a study carried out by Brunel University in 2022.

However, campaigners and veterans have accused the MoD of withholding full health records, including blood and urine tests, which they say would establish a link.

The MoD released some official documents in July 2026 , though it said some records may have been inadvertently destroyed three years earlier.

The department also said the medical records that veterans and their families were trying to access would appear "complex and inconsistent" as a central database was never held by the military, in part due to the intense Cold War-era security around the nuclear tests.

Burnham told MPs medical for the veterans do exist and it was "indefensible" they have been withheld.

'Serious allegations against the state'

The independent panel announced on Tuesday will be be modelled on the Hillsborough Independent Panel and chaired by the same person, James Jones, the former Bishop of Liverpool.

He told BBC Newsnight: "The nuclear veterans have for decades made serious allegations against the state about what happened to them and to their descendants through the exposure to nuclear radiation. These merit serious investigation."

Downing Street said it would produce a report by October 2027 to coincide with the 75th anniversary of the first British nuclear weapons test.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "It's taken too long to get here and I think today of the people who haven't lived to see this moment - and I fear for the people who might not see the outcome."

He acknowledged low trust in the MoD among veterans and their families, assuring them the department would not be involved with setting up the panel or defining its remit.

He said the panel would "help us to make sure that the cover-up is exposed".

Asked if the government would pay compensation should the panel recommend it, Streeting said he would not pre-judge its report but that he felt "absolutely sure the findings will be uncomfortable" and the government "will have to take that on the chin".

stories.title: Reality TV star backs extending sex education to 18
stories.summary: Georgia Harrison, who was a victim of "revenge porn", says children are exposed to online "poison".
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Georgia Harrison says young people are being exposed to "poison" online

Published 9 hours ago

TV celebrity and "revenge porn" victim Georgia Harrison has urged MPs to back a new law that would extend compulsory relationships and sex education (RSE) up to the age of 18.

The Only Way Is Essex and Love Island star led a protest outside Parliament to call for the change, telling the BBC it was needed to combat the "poison" young people were being exposed to online.

The demonstration comes ahead of a debate and vote next week on a draft law that would legally require all further education providers in England to teach RSE to under-18s.

The Department for Education (DfE) said it was exploring how RSE could be extended to colleges.

Compulsory relationships and sex education currently stops at age 16 in England, meaning sixth forms and colleges are not required to teach the subject.

Speaking in Westminster, Harrison said: "Between 16 and 18 is the age that people first start having sex.

"It doesn't make sense that we're abandoning them at that time."

Harrison said "misogynists" had "sold our young people advice, but really, it's poison".

"We need to undo it and the only way to undo it is through education," Harrison said.

Harrison was a victim of so-called revenge porn . Fellow reality TV performer Stephen Bear was jailed for posting intimate footage of the pair online, which he had filmed at his home in Loughton in Essex.

She said making RSE mandatory to age 18 could help prevent intimate image abuse of the kind she suffered.

The campaign outside Parliament was organised by media organisation LADbible.

The Relationships and Sex Education (Further Education Sector) Bill has been put forward by Alistair Strathern, the Labour MP for the Hitchin constituency in Bedfordshire and Hertfordshire.

It is a private members' bill, which are only debated on Fridays and rarely become law.

However, Strathern told the BBC he had "a good chance of making real change".

"I've been really encouraged by the response we've got from ministers so far," he said.

Georgia Harrison, pictured with Alistair Strathern MP, says stopping sex education at 16 "doesn't make sense"

A DfE spokesperson said: "Supporting children and young people to grow up happy and healthy whilst safeguarding them from harm on and offline is a job for us all.

"We're determined that across our education system, schools and colleges play their part.

"That's why we have rolled out mandatory RHSE [relationships, sex and health education] in schools and we are exploring how we can extend this to colleges too."

The bill follows a petition by the survivor-led campaign group Make it Mandatory, which called for sex education to be mandated to 18.

Faustine Petron said she founded the campaign after surviving a coercive and abusive relationship when she was under 18.

"I thought back to the lack of education I had about the signs of abusive behaviour, grooming and coercive control," Petron said.

"I was shocked in my research to find out that sex education ends at 16. I thought 'how nonsensical'.

"I got into the relationship at 16. Why stop and have this dangerous loophole in the law?"

stories.body:
Several members of chat set up after alleged murder of Feng Jianming say they or their parents were called by police from their home towns in China

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Chinese police have contacted several people who were part of a WeChat group that discussed attending a Melbourne vigil for Feng Jianming, the HungryPanda food delivery rider allegedly murdered this month.

At least three members of the group set up after Feng’s death said they had been contacted, raising concerns that Chinese authorities may have been alerted to discussions about the protest activity either automatically or manually by the Chinese-owned messaging and social app.

Feng was allegedly stabbed to death near Queen Victoria market on the evening of Friday 6 November after he and another rider confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes.

Angry members of the WeChat group set up in the immediate aftermath volunteered to host a vigil for the 49-year-old rider at the State Library of Victoria the next day, amid broader concerns about the treatment of riders by the company .

The group’s chat history, seen by Guardian Australia, shows that by Wednesday at least three members had told the group that they or their parents had been called by police officers from their home towns in China asking about their involvement with the vigil. The group, which by then had more than 400 members, was disbanded the next day after participants expressed fears about the police calls.

Members of the chat group declined to speak on the record, citing safety concerns.

HungryPanda, founded in the UK, targets the Chinese expatriate market in 10 countries. In Australia, it operates in nine cities, including Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Adelaide.

The Melbourne incident mirrored an event in February when HungryPanda riders in Sydney were contacted by police in China after a WeChat discussion about a proposed strike over wages on lunar new year’s eve.

More than half the WeChat group’s 155 members left and the strike was abandoned after the calls from police, which were first reported by the ABC .

Joy Wang, a former HungryPanda rider who was in the February group chat, said she had received four police calls from her home town in Henan province.

Wang said the police seemed unaware that the protest was in Sydney. When she explained this, she said they had threatened her with reprisals if she went back to China.

“They said, ‘You better not attend the protest, or we could go after you when you return to China,’” Wang said.

Jack (not his real name), who quit HungryPanda two years ago and now runs his own business in eastern China, said he had joined the February WeChat group to show support to his former colleagues. He had received three calls from police in his home town and was told not to take part in the strike.

Jack then quit the group chat. “I’m currently in China, there are things I need to consider,” he said.

Kitty Lu, the global spokesperson for HungryPanda, said the company had no responsibility for riders being contacted by Chinese police. The company was privately owned and independently operated, with funding from private and institutional investors in Europe and North America, she said.

Wang said the group members in Australia who were called by police had registered with WeChat under their Chinese mobile numbers.

She believed the use of keywords such as “strike” in the chat may have been the trigger for the messages to be transmitted to the Chinese authorities.

Jeffrey Knockel, a senior research fellow at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, agreed. He and his colleagues studied a 2016 wage protest in Jiangsu province and found that the phrase “industrial strike across the city” in the organisers’ group chat activated an automated mechanism on WeChat.

He suggested something similar may have happened in the Australian cases. Knockel also argued that WeChat may have flagged the group chat to a Chinese government organisation that would have then traced the riders’ details on China’s family registration system, known as hukou , and instructed local police to contact them.

WeChat has previously said that the data of foreign users is stored in Singapore, beyond the reach of Chinese authorities, but Knockel said if one member of a group registered their account with a Chinese number, the whole chat could be monitored by Chinese authorities.

after newsletter promotion

WeChat did not respond to a request for comment.

Kevin Slaten, who leads the China Dissent Monitor at the US-based thinktank Freedom House, also thought the February calls might have been triggered by WeChat, given a rise in the number of labour disputes about wages in China during 2025 and early 2026.

“[The Chinese authorities may have] just assumed that these workers were in this wave of wage protests … not knowing initially that they weren’t physically located in China,” Slaten said.

But as the security apparatus was under direction to pay special attention to wage protests, the police may have persisted in warning riders to halt their action, even after learning they were overseas, he said.

The executive director of China Labor Watch, Qiang Li, has documented several cases of Chinese workers abroad being contacted by Chinese authorities after using WeChat to discuss industrial action. But these workers were usually working for projects controlled by China’s state companies.

Li said Chinese police had “overreacted” in the HungryPanda case but it was still alarming for Australia.

“Today we see these riders being called by Chinese police,” he said. “We could then see cases of anyone who uses WeChat, including Australian enforcement officials, their families, or anyone related to China, to be surveilled through this system.”

The home affairs department said it could not comment on operational matters but a spokesperson said it was “unacceptable for any foreign government to target members of our community to prevent individuals exercising their fundamental rights and freedoms in Australia”.

“Acts of harassment, assault, unwanted surveillance, intimidation, coercion or other threatening behaviour may constitute criminal offences.”

The opposition home affairs spokesperson, Jonathon Duniam, called on the government to do more to address the potential use of WeChat for surveillance.

“The Coalition has raised serious concerns about WeChat’s links to the Chinese Communist party, its censorship practices and its potential use for surveillance, yet the Albanese government has not done enough to address these risks or ensure proper transparency and accountability from the platform,” he said.

In 2023, a Senate inquiry into foreign interference recommended banning WeChat on government devices and establishing a national security technology office to monitor “high-risk” social media groups, including WeChat.

The government said only that it “noted” these recommendations.

The Chinese embassy in Canberra declined to comment on the HungryPanda allegations.

stories.title: None of UK government's £2.5bn steel package spent in Wales, figures show
stories.summary: Wales is home to the UK's largest steelworks which is currently transitioning to an electric arc furnace.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
A new electric furnace is due to be up and running at Port Talbot by the end of 2027

Published 24 November 2026

Wales has not received any money from the UK government's £2.5bn steel industry investment plan announced in February 2025, according to figures obtained through a Freedom of Information (FOI) request.

The UK's Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade confirmed that "the government has not spent, nor allocated, nor committed any money under the £2.5bn commitment in Wales".

The FOI was obtained by the Liberal Democrats, whose Welsh leader David Chadwick said that Welsh Labour MPs needed to "demand a fair share for Welsh steel now, before their own government spends the rest".

The UK government said it had "invested extensively to secure steelmaking" in Port Talbot.

The department's FOI response noted that £751m had been invested in the nationalised British Steel site in Scunthorpe and another £172m spent stepping in to save Specialist Steel UK in south Yorkshire and the West Midlands.

Wales is home to Port Talbot's Tata Steel site, the largest steelworks in the UK, which closed its last blast furnace in September 2024 .

A new electric furnace is due to be up and running at the site by the end of 2027, but there are concerns it could now be delayed due to grid connection issues .

Speaking on 24 February 2025, following the announcement of the new steel investment plan, the then-Labour energy minister Sarah Jones said the £2.5bn "could benefit regions across the UK - like Scunthorpe, Rotherham, Redcar, Yorkshire and Port Talbot - which have a strong history of steel production".

She added the money would be "spent on initiatives that would give the industry a long future - such as supporting the transition to electric arc furnaces or other improvements in UK capabilities".

As of October, the UK government had spent £751m on sustaining British Steel in Scunthorpe, since ministers took it into full public ownership in July 2025.

But the National Audit Office warned in March that spending on the site could exceed £1.5bn by 2028 , external .

The £172m spent on Specialist Steel UK has funded things such as ongoing site safety and wages, since the company entered liquidation in August 2026.

In September the UK government announced plans to nationalise the business , which has sites in south Yorkshire and the West Midlands.

In September 2024, Tata Steel in Port Talbot was promised a £500m subsidy from the UK government towards a new electric arc furnace, alongside a commitment by Tata Steel to invest £700m of its own money .

That investment was a conditional grant, not part of the £2.5bn steel industry investment fund announced in 2025.

Port Talbot is home to the largest steelworks in the UK

In March 2026 Plaid Cymru MP Ben Lake asked how much of the £2.5bn steel industry fund would be spent in Wales, to which the then-minister in the Department for Business and Trade, Chris McDonald, said the Welsh secretary would have a role in attracting investment for Welsh steel projects.

"The National Wealth Fund will be the UK government's main mechanism for providing financing for investment in the steel sector.

"Investment decisions are made by the National Wealth Fund on a case-by-case basis and it supports promising projects across the United Kingdom," he said.

"Specifically for Wales, the Secretary of State for Wales will convene the National Wealth Fund and the private sector in a new initiative to help attract investment to Welsh steel projects, to support communities across Wales that rely on the industry."

Chadwick said the lack of investment into Wales from the plan was "the latest in a long line of Labour betrayals of Wales".

"Labour was happy to talk about saving Welsh steel when it wanted Welsh votes," he said. "Now we know what those promises were worth.

"They'll put Wales in the press release, pose in a hard hat in Port Talbot and tell us how much they care. Yet, so far, they haven't delivered a single penny to Wales from their much-lauded steel fund."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham was asked by Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey in Prime Ministers Questions "why on Earth" no money had been spent in Wales and whether Burnham would meet him and Chadwick "to put right this latest betrayal of Welsh industry and jobs"?

Burnham said there was "more to be done" on supporting Port Talbot's steel industry.

He added: "On the steel industry and particularly in Wales... the government has invested heavily in Tata steel in Port Talbot in the electric arc furnace .

"We have as a government invested heavily in steel transition in south Wales".

A UK government spokesperson said it had "invested extensively to secure steelmaking in Port Talbot, in local jobs and in the future of the town.

"This includes £500m to support the £1.25bn transformation of Tata Steel Port Talbot into a modern electric arc steelworks, £102m direct government support for workers and businesses affected by Tata's transition, £64m towards upgrading the port and £14.8m into town centre regeneration.

The spokesperson added the government had also committed to invest up to £2.5bn rebuilding the UK steel industry, including through the National Wealth Fund, "which welcomes applications that meet its criteria from companies in Wales and across the UK, and our steel strategy is also delivering for Welsh steelmakers".

State-run Global Times says reports about CEO’s affair with alleged Chinese spy were ‘malicious’

Trump made up to $15m on Nvidia stock after Huang’s return

Nvidia staff: what do you think of Jensen Huang’s return as chief executive?

Chinese media have reacted with glee to the dramatic reinstatement of Jensen Huang as the chief executive of Nvidia, with one commentary warning against future “witch-hunts”.

An article published on Tuesday in the state-run outlet the Global Times said US media reports about Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset were “malicious” and “negatively impacted American public perception of China”.

Huang was reinstated to the US artificial intelligence company on Tuesday, weeks after he was ousted by the board after allegations that he had three affairs , including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with employees. But the Nvidia board reinstated him after an intervention from Donald Trump.

The Global Times warned that future “political witch-hunts” against companies and individuals accused of links to Chinese intelligence could take the form of investigations and congressional hearings.

“Certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering [sic],” it said.

In another article, the influential blogger Niu Tanqin wrote that Huang’s return indicated that the “so-called female spy allegations are complete nonsense”.

Niu also said that China would be flattered by Donald Trump’s suggestion, made in an interview with CNBC, that Huang could be poached by China.

The US president said on Monday that Xi Jinping, China’s leader, described Huang as a “brilliant man” in their recent meeting in Shenzhen, a city in southern China.

Trump said that, despite the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s affair with the alleged China intelligence asset Alice Huang – no relation – “the bigger threat would be losing the brainpower of somebody like Jensen”.

Nvidia produces the world’s most advanced semiconductors, which underpin the artificial intelligence sector. US export controls have blocked Nvidia from shipping its most sophisticated models to China in a bid to slow down the country’s AI development. Huang has pushed for looser regulations, arguing that it is better to keep China dependent on US technology rather than spur Chinese innovation.

Trump said he had personally intervened with the Nvidia board, which had previously ruled out reinstating Huang. “I spoke to them, let me put it that way,” Trump told CNBC on Monday. “And I convinced them … I made the deal.”

Huang’s comeback caused Nvidia’s shares to soar on Monday, adding almost $1tn (£763bn) in market value to the company, which props up much of the US stock markets.

Senator Tom Cotton, the Republican chair of the intelligence committee, said : “I have warned the administration from the start about communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access. “The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it’s not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back,” he said.

China’s foreign ministry declined to comment on Huang’s reinstatement. The government has consistently denied the espionage allegations, calling them “slander and defamation”.

Several accounts on Chinese social media shared memes and AI-generated videos showing Huang in various revenge scenarios. In one video, shared by an influential blogger, with more than 1.1 million followers, Huang is reimagined in the Arnold Schwarzenegger movie The Terminator, in the famous “I’ll be back” scene.

In another video, Huang is reimagined as Jack Nicholson’s murderous Jack Torrance in the 1980 horror film The Shining. Huang is shown using an axe to destroy a locked bathroom door, terrorising an AI-generated Colette Kress, who was Nvidia’s interim boss , who is cowering behind it. The video ends with an AI-generated “Here’s Jensen!” channelling Nicholson’s famous line, “Here’s Johnny!”, from the movie.

Analysts believe that the saga also demonstrated to Beijing how power works in the US.

“The lesson Chinese policymakers are likely drawing is neither subtle nor complicated: Donald Trump remains the most influential political figure in America and, in many respects, the most consequential variable in the trajectory of US-China relations,” wrote George Chen, a partner at The Asia Group, a consultancy, in a post on Substack.

stories.title: Ministers ask public for views on changing age of consent
stories.summary: Some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

The UK government is inviting the public to share its views as ministers consider whether or not to stagger the age of consent.

Currently adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds, however some campaigners have argued that different limits should apply, depending on the age gap between the people involved.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he wanted survivors, parents, young people, victim support services and the wider public "to share their experiences and inform this process".

The government is also announcing that new limits on non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) will come into force months earlier than originally planned.

The measures, which will now become law in January 2027, invalidate confidentiality clauses in new NDAs if they prevent employees from talking about harassment or discrimination or victims from reporting criminal conduct.

The changes will also cover NDAs signed outside of the workplace and mean that even if victims of crime have signed an NDA, it would not stop them from speaking to anyone, including the media, about what had happened.

Zelda Perkins, founder of the group Can't Buy My Silence, said the laws would "uphold the integrity of a legal system that must never be used to protect perpetrators at the expense of victims".

Perkins has previously said she felt forced to sign an NDA, which prevented her talking about abuse carried out by her former boss, the film producer Harvey Weinstein.

In 2017, she told the BBC she had tried to speak out about Weinstein's behaviour towards a co-worker but was told by lawyers she "didn't have a chance" due to signing an NDA.

Writing in the Guardian, , external Burnham said: "NDAs should protect sensitive business information or commercial interests. They should not protect powerful men who have abused, harassed or discriminated against women."

He added he would "keep working to make sure NDAs can't be used to silence others, including freelancers employees and fans who experience abuse".

The government has also said it is actively looking at whether to change the law on the age of consent and that it will ask members of the public for their opinions in the new year.

Burnham said: "I not only want to make sure victims can speak out about their own abuse, but also have the opportunity to challenge the status quo."

The Close the Consent Gap campaign is proposing that 16-year-olds would not be able to have a sexual relationship with anyone older than 19, and that someone aged 17 would be prohibited from a relationship with anyone older than 20.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson said there is a question about what is considered "appropriate" for 16 and 17-year-olds.

She said: "I think some of the cases that we've seen where you have a huge age difference and often where you've got a much older adult man, who is in a position of authority, having a relationship with a 16 or 17-year-old makes me feel deeply uncomfortable."

She added: "I think we do need to look at that, but it's complex, we want to look at all of the options and we'll be setting out more and making sure survivors, women's groups and others are involved in that so we can get this right."

Earlier this month, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said there was "some common sense" about staggering the age of consent but questioned whether a new law could be enforced.

She also said it was "very confusing" to see Labour ministers talk about staggering the age of consent for sexual relations while at the same time lowering the voting age to 16.

Scotland's justice secretary Neil Gray earlier this month said the Scottish government would "consider carefully any evidence-based proposals intended to strengthen protections for young people" when asked about a staggered approach.

He also said there were "no current plans" to change the general position of the age of consent being 16.

A complication with changing the age of consent in Scotland is how it would affect marriage law which allows people to marry or enter a civil partnership at 16. The legal age of marriage in England and Wales is 18.

Some countries around the world have a staggered age of consent. In Canada , external the age of consent for sexual activity is 16 years-old but a 14 or 15-year-old can consent to sexual activity as long as the partner is less than five years older.

Staggered age of consent to be discussed after Brand case, minister says Published 15 November

Recent high-profile cases including Russell Brand's rape conviction and allegations made against David Walliams have prompted conversations about both the age of consent and NDAs.

Mia Latter, a woman who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and he was 30, has called for the age of consent to be changed.

Latter is one of six women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Brand denied the allegations at the time and none of the six women were complainants in Brand's recent criminal trial.

Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Latter said she was "delighted" the government was considering whether to stagger the age of consent, describing it as a "step in the right direction".

In the same week that Brand was convicted, ITV News and the Guardian reported that David Walliams had been accused of sexual misconduct by several women.

One woman said she now characterises her alleged encounter with Walliams at 15 years old as a "sexual assault". Walliams strongly denied he had any sexual contact with the girl.

Walliams said he rejected any allegations of criminal activity and that he has never engaged in the grooming of young women.

In late 2023, Walliams' publisher HarperCollins started an internal inquiry about the author's alleged inappropriate behaviour with young female staff.

A female staff member left the company with a pay-out and an NDA.

A spokesperson for the publisher has said: "HarperCollins UK previously terminated its publishing relationship with David Walliams.

"We take the safety of our people incredibly seriously and to respect the privacy of individuals we do not comment on employee matters."

stories.body:
Trump’s reaction to sensitive information that contradicts his worldview mirrors his conduct towards war with Iran

Donald Trump’s unwillingness to heed warnings of suspected Chinese penetration of the tech giant Nvidia follows a pattern of the US president ignoring sensitive intelligence that contradicts his world view.

Trump disregarded repeated information that the company’s co-founder, Jensen Huang , was having an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy that threatened to undermine Washington’s geostrategically vital goal of pipping China for global supremacy in the artificial intelligence race.

The woman, Alice Huang – no blood relation of Jensen – was also responsible for buying $4.8bn worth of Nvidia’s highly sensitive AI chips in her capacity as head of a Singapore-based technology company, Megaspeed. The chips were then diverted to China, despite US export restrictions forbidding such sales to a country Washington regards as a key strategic adversary.

The president was inactive even after Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security adviser – and one of the administration’s renowned “China hawks” – repackaged the intelligence into a classified report last May warning of the geopolitical risks posed by the relationship.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action against what was an emerging and then eventually very clear chip diversion network that was emerging under Megaspeed and other south-east Asian offshore data farms – and it just failed to act,” said Julia Curlee, a former Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) officer who specialized in the Middle East and China and also worked on the White House national security council during Trump’s first presidency.

“It’s the latest episode of the president ignoring or not believing the intelligence that’s being provided to him.”

Despite the intelligence concerns raised by his conduct, Huang was reinstated as Nvidia’s chief executive on Monday following pressure from the White House and the company’s shareholders.

Trump’s behaviour over the Nvidia affairs mirrors his conduct towards the war with Iran, Curlee argues, where he pressed ahead with military actions despite being forewarned of potential complications.

Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran contradicted advice that the country’s Islamic regime had the resilience to withstand attempts to topple it and was likely to retaliate by closing the strait of Hormuz – predictions that were subsequently borne out.

Trump’s dismissal of intelligence warnings in both cases recalls his comments at a 2018 summit with Vladimir Putin when he openly sided with the Russian president over US intelligence agencies, who had assessed that Russia had interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

His indifference to intelligence work and the professionals who perform it appears to surpass that of previous administrations, even those who were accused of deliberately politicizing the practice – an accusation leveled at George W Bush following the 2003 invasion of Iraq.

“There are other administrations that have ignored or or tried to politicize intelligence but I think the Trump administration stands alone in how little it seems to regard the intelligence analysis prepared to help the president make decisions,” said Curlee.

“The best example of this is the run-up to the war in Iran, where the administration just truly shut out the warnings which have been there and were provided for many years about what the Iranians would do in the case of a war.”

Trump’s administration has also fired agents for providing intelligence assessments at odds with the president’s own statements. Last year, Lt Gen Jeffrey Kruse, the head of the Defense Intelligence Agency, was dismissed over a report that contradicted Trump’s claim that Iran’s nuclear sites had been “obliterated” by US strikes carried out in June 2025.

“What makes them really different from, say, the Bush administration, is that even that administration did not publicly fire officers when they didn’t provide information the president wanted to hear,” said Curlee, who also served on the White House national security council under Trump and Joe Biden.

“I feel pretty strongly that the fault of the Iran war lies at this refusal to listen to the intelligence community.”

Curlee said the Chinese acquisition of the Nvidia chips compared in strategic significance to the case of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg , a US couple who were executed after being convicted of passing on atomic secrets to the Soviet Union in the early years of the cold war. That made official indifference to the intelligence discovery all the more remarkable, she argued.

“This is a technology at the heart of the strategic competition with our primary competitor in the world, and at an industrial scale, they managed to divert chips from our leading hardware company,” she said.

“It’s a terrible thing that’s occurred and we can’t undo that. But uncovering it and stopping it was done at least over a year ago. If the policymaker then refuses to do their job, there’s nothing the intelligence community can do about that.”

The administration’s stance has drawn further scrutiny by deciding not to provide a “defensive briefing” to Jensen Huang about the discovery.

“Before public accusations and scandals, it used to be accepted practice for someone to pull the American target aside for a man-to-man chat – to tell him to think with the head between his shoulders,” said Fulton Armstrong, a former CIA analyst specializing in Latin America who also has experience in Taiwan.

“The chat might even include discussion of feeding the foreigner some disinformation. It seems that four years of Trump’s first presidency, four years of do-nothingism with Biden, and now almost two years of Trump II have so deeply changed the intel community that practical solutions are no longer allowed.”

No explanation has been provided for the failure to warn Huang – thus allowing him to continue his relationship with Alice Huang. He was also allowed to maintain his already close access to Trump.

Curlee said it was a “policy decision [rather than] an intelligence decision.” She added “It is to me a very unusual suspect decision to let something like this go on for as long as it apparently did, without at minimum protecting this US citizen, who is the object of of a Chinese spy operation.”

Fevered speculation has swirled over whether Alice Huang may have been part of a “honey trap” operation set by China’s intelligence services to lure Jensen Huang into a close business relationship that would entice him into sending vast amounts of Nvidia’s coveted chips to a company which would them to pass them to China, subverting American law.

China’s sprawling ministry of state security (MSS) is believed to use the technique, which most western intelligence agencies publicly insist they do not use, on the grounds that is unethical and potentially counterproductive, because it often depends on blackmail.

But analysts doubt that it occurred in this instance. Alice Huang, they suggest, could have disclosed the relationship to Chinese agents after it began because she was legally obliged to do so under China’s catch-all intelligence law, which legally obliges the country’s citizens to “cooperate” with security services on matters defined as “national security”. That term has a much broader definition under China’s laws than in most western countries, and can cover commercial and economic development issues.

Frank Montoya, a retired FBI agent who specialized on China, said a straightforward “honey trap” was unlikely.

“I don’t think that it was it was mapped out specifically where the MSS officer said we’re going to find this person and we’re going to set her up for business and then target her against against the CEO of [Nvidia],” he said.

“There was a confluence of opportunities. She’s very ambitious, very smart and she has this idea, and doesn’t necessarily brings it to the MSS, but is talking to somebody else. She has connections in the party, and she’s talking to somebody else, and then somebody else talks to the MSS and says, ‘Hey, let’s see if we can take advantage of that’.”

He added: “This was a multibillion-dollar purchase [of Nvidia chips]. There’s no way the MSS alone can fund that. They’re going to need somebody higher up [in the Chinese Communist party] to not only approve that but to provide the money when the deal is made.”

The operation, Montoya said, bore the hallmarks of the Chinese espionage approach, which he described as “whole of government” and lacking the “clandestinity” of traditional spycraft.

Alice Huang would have drawn the attention of US intelligence agencies through Megaspeed’s mass purchase of Nvidia chips, and because it rented out services from its Singapore datacenters to Chinese AI companies, Curlee argues.

The intimate nature of her relationship with Jensen Huang and her links to Chinese intelligence are thought to have been discovered through surveillance of her phone, almost certainly carried out by the National Security Agency.

Trump has dismissed the case’s importance, saying he does not believe US national security was threatened and telling Fox News: “We spy on China. They spy on us.” He later told reporters that he raised the matter only briefly when he met China’s president, Xi Jinping, at last week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) gathering Shenzhen.

It is an attitude Curlee lamented as disdainful of intelligence as a whole.

“We are spending tens of billions of dollars and people put their lives in jeopardy to collect information at great personal risk so that our leaders have decision-advantage, the ability to anticipate crises around the corner and can respond to foreign threats,” she said. “If the president can’t be bothered to listen to his intelligence community then what is what is the point of it all?”

stories.body:
The US and Russia lack the power to impose their will on the continent – the Shenzhen summit was no Yalta 2.0

T he first ever trilateral summit between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin was rich in symbolism and empty of substance. Many Europeans, filled with anxiety about the Chinese, Russian and US presidents potentially colluding, saw chilling echoes of the Yalta conference in 1945, when Joseph Stalin, Winston Churchill and Franklin D Roosevelt redrew the map of Europe.

But those – particularly in eastern Europe – who are fretting about another historic betrayal should remember that when it comes to European security today, we are the ones who hold most of the cards. Far more meaningful last week than Shenzhen was a gathering in Berlin , held at exactly the same time.

True, the Shenzhen summit brought together three autocratic leaders who would like to see the world carved up into spheres of influence, but their meeting turned out to be no Yalta 2.0. The original Yalta took place as the second world war drew to a close, when international law and multilateral organisations were little more than a pipedream. The world was still living in an age of empire, with many colonies in the hands of European countries and the Soviet Union eager to consolidate its own in eastern Europe . It was hardly surprising, back then, that the war’s victors, the US, the UK and the USSR, held the keys to Europe’s future.

Nothing of the kind was ever going to happen in Shenzhen, nor will it at any future gathering of Xi, Trump and Putin alone. Two of the three – Putin and Trump – cannot win the wars they have launched against Ukraine and Iran respectively. The third, Xi, by far the strongest of the trio, is doing little more than bask in the colossal mistakes of his American and Russian friends.

This is not to say that the three are irrelevant to Europe’s security. Russia and the US hold the world’s largest nuclear arsenals. Had Trump, Putin and Xi committed to nuclear arms control, as Trump wanted , Europe (and the rest of the world) would have applauded. But the Russian and Chinese leaders were never going to indulge Trump on that score. Possessing nuclear weapons is the only reason Putin can still claim a seat at the top table; without them, Russia would be little more than a second-rate power. China, meanwhile, in its scramble for superpower status, is racing to expand its nuclear arsenal, and catch up with the US and Russia.

Russia, China and the US also matter in other dimensions of security. Putin’s Russia continues its military assault on Ukraine, which faces its hardest winter since Russia invaded. And Russia’s cyber-attacks, drone incursions, sabotage, attacks on critical infrastructure and disinformation campaigns across Europe have escalated to the point that it makes little sense to keep talking about “hybrid war”, or even “shadow war”. It would perhaps be more honest simply to call it what it is: Russia’s war against Europe.

Russia is hardly fighting this war alone. China is not a direct participant, but has provided economic and technological support that has been vital to Russia’s war machine. Yet for all their efforts, there is no sign that Ukraine, or indeed any other European country, will fold – and this despite the fact that Trump’s US has all but switched sides. Washington no longer provides economic or military support to Ukraine. And while it still cooperates on intelligence and satellite communications, it has sickeningly tried to pressure Kyiv into capitulating by temporarily cutting off or slowing down these services. The US still has the capacity to inflict real damage on Ukraine and Europe. But Trump has failed to subjugate Ukraine over the last two years, and given his Republican party’s bruising defeat in the US midterm elections, he is unlikely to succeed in the next two.

Trump, Putin and Xi may like a world in which, to borrow from Thucydides, the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. Their agreement in Shenzhen to oppose the alleged overreach of international tribunals – established precisely to disprove that might makes right – signals exactly this. But the three men are not as strong as they would like to believe, nor is today’s world the Hobbesian wasteland over which Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin had the power to rule unchallenged. International law and multilateralism are under attack – but they are not dead. Middle powers in the global south are rising and making their voices heard.

after newsletter promotion

And Europe, though facing serious security threats, has far more leverage than is often recognised. Last week’s meeting in Berlin – where representatives of 36 countries in the French- and British-led coalition of the willing gathered to shore up support for Ukraine – was a show of strength far more concrete than the empty words in Shenzhen.

The group agreed to close Ukraine’s funding gap for 2027: the EU has pledged an additional €45bn , with a further €25bn coming from non-EU coalition members such as the UK, Norway and Canada. And while the last time the EU agreed on a loan to Ukraine guaranteed by the EU budget, it allowed Hungary and Slovakia to opt out, today it is in no mood to tolerate dropouts. With negotiations on the next seven-year EU budget entering a critical phase, Germany, the largest net contributor, will oppose any budget deal unless all EU members agree to support Ukraine.

Europe’s main problem is not material but political and, above all, psychological. Learned helplessness, towards the US in particular, is what fuels fears of the ghosts of Yalta, and a new betrayal. And it is because Europe still takes the Trump-Putin peace-talks charade too seriously that it spends so much time squabbling over who should represent it at that table.

No peace plan pushed through by Putin and Trump will deliver Ukraine’s surrender, let alone a new security architecture for Europe. On their own, they lack the power to impose their will. The more energy Europe devotes to delivering on the plans and pledges of the coalition of the willing, and the less it spends chasing the two failing leaders in Moscow and Washington, the more secure and peaceful tomorrow’s Europe will be.

Nathalie Tocci is a professor of practice at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies, Europe, and a senior fellow at Bocconi University’s Institute for European Policymaking
