stories.body:
After the president’s meeting with Putin and Xi, the US must take the lead in restoring arms control agreements

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping met last week in southern China, where Trump said they would “talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization”.

It was the first time the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers had come together to discuss the future of nuclear weapons. That discussion was long overdue.

But in typical Trump fashion, this meeting was all pomp and little pop. If Trump wants to make the world safer, he needs to do more than talk. The US needs to lead.

Nuclear weapons remain the greatest immediate threat to the security of the US, Russia, China and the entire world. As the risks of artificial intelligence, climate emergency and geopolitical instability grow, the danger of nuclear catastrophe has not diminished. In fact, the erosion of arms control agreements and the modernization and expansion of nuclear arsenals are bringing us closer to a dangerous new arms race.

The first priority must be rebuilding the arms control architecture that the United States and Russia spent half a century constructing. During and after the cold war, Washington and Moscow negotiated a series of treaties that helped prevent nuclear confrontation and reduced their nuclear arsenals by roughly 88%.

Those agreements demonstrated that even adversaries can find common ground when the stakes are existential.

But that progress is now in jeopardy.

The New Start Treaty, the last remaining agreement limiting the strategic nuclear arsenals of the United States and Russia, expired earlier this year without a replacement. Today, there are no legally binding limits on the size of their nuclear arsenals and China has never been subject to comparable restrictions.

The result is a growing risk of a three-way nuclear arms race that would make all three countries – and the world – less safe.

There were plenty of reasons to be skeptical that this meeting could produce meaningful results. Trump likes to talk about “denuclearization”, but talk is not a strategy.

During his first administration, Trump tried to bring China into bilateral nuclear arms control negotiations between Washington and Moscow. That effort failed because Beijing correctly pointed out that it had a much smaller arsenal than the others.

China is expanding its nuclear arsenal, but it possesses roughly 600 nuclear weapons, compared with approximately 4,000 in the arsenals of both the US and Russia. Expecting Beijing to negotiate reductions on the same terms as Washington and Moscow is simply unrealistic. We cannot make progress by demanding that China reduce its arsenal while the US and Russia retain arsenals many times larger.

Nor should Trump wait for Putin to make the first move. Putin has increasingly relied on nuclear threats to discourage other countries from supporting Ukraine and to advance his broader strategic objectives. But even though he may resist reductions, that does not mean Russia wants to spend the next decade locked in another costly nuclear arms race.

In fact, shortly before New Start expired, Moscow proposed that the United States and Russia voluntarily maintain their existing limits on strategic nuclear weapons while negotiating a successor agreement. Trump rejected that proposal.

That was a missed opportunity. Trump should reverse course and put that proposal back on the table.

If Trump wants to make real progress, he needs to change his tune and lead the band. He should immediately agree with Putin to freeze their nuclear arsenals while negotiating a new arms control agreement to replace New Start.

And we should aim higher than simply restoring the status quo. A new agreement should reduce American and Russian nuclear arsenals to 1,000 weapons each, counting both strategic (long-range) weapons and tactical (shorter-range) weapons. Such reductions would lower the risk of nuclear war, rebuild a measure of trust between Washington and Moscow, and save taxpayers billions of dollars that would otherwise be spent building and maintaining weapons we do not need.

Just as importantly, a serious American-Russian agreement would create the conditions for China to join the process. Beijing should commit to refraining from further significant increases in its nuclear arsenal as long as Washington and Moscow are making real progress toward substantial reductions.

The objective should be straightforward: bring American and Russian arsenals down toward China’s level, not drive China to build up toward ours. That is how we prevent a three-way arms race before it gets started.

Some will argue that the United States must maintain nuclear superiority over China and should never reduce its arsenal unless Beijing agrees to comparable reductions. But that approach mistakes nuclear superiority for nuclear security.

History demonstrates that arms control works when countries negotiate from a position of mutual security and seek stability, rather than endlessly pursuing an advantage over one another.

A new nuclear arms race among the US, Russia and China would serve nobody’s interests. It would waste enormous sums of public money, accelerate environmental damage, undermine international security and increase the possibility that a crisis or miscalculation could end in nuclear catastrophe.

The world does not need another nuclear arms race. It needs leadership, diplomacy, and a clear commitment to a safer future. If Trump is serious about denuclearization, moving forward, he now has his chance to prove it.

Edward J Markey represents Massachusetts in the US Senate. He is a co-chair of the bicameral congressional nuclear weapons and arms control working group

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

Published 24 November 2026

US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.

Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.

Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.

Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.

"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.

With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia Published 23 hours ago

The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .

But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.

"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

"Obviously, if Nvidia was the target or was subject to some criminal investigation or they were obstructing or thwarting our investigation, then that wouldn't be the message that the president is saying to the American people.

"It shouldn't be what my message would be either."

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.

The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Published 1 day ago

The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, its chairman, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".

The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

On Monday, Trump said he had spoken to the company's directors and convinced them to bring back Huang .

Huang's reinstatement provoked bipartisan anger.

Republican Congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".

Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".

Democratic Senator Ruben Gallego said Congress needed to "investigate what stock positions took place before the announcement".

Temporary quotas on vehicles entering the bloc will also apply to cars from the UK, Japan and Turkey

The EU will next month impose its threatened caps on the number of Chinese hybrid cars that can be imported into the bloc, the European Commission has announced.

The quotas will also apply to hybrids from Japan, Turkey, South Korea and the UK, but the principal purpose is to limit imports from China after an agreement with Beijing in October that has led to a rise in exports to the bloc.

The quota, under World Trade Organization rules, is temporary and will apply for 200 days from 1 December during an investigation into imports of plug-in and battery-powered hybrid vehicles. The EU is attempting to cut its huge trade deficit with China.

“In view of the sensitivity of the hybrids sector, its strategic importance to the union economy in terms of innovation, electrification and employment, and the existence of sufficient evidence showing that imports of hybrids threaten to cause serious injury to the union industry,” the official journal said on Tuesday.

It will limit tariff-free imports of Chinese vehicles to 350,000 in the first year or about 191,000 over 200 days.

First-year quotas would be set at 310,000 for Japan, 230,000 for Turkey, 105,000 for South Korea and 190,000 for the UK, which last year exported 166,000 hybrids to the EU.

The quota amounts to about half of the number of Chinese hybrids expected to be imported to the EU in the next 12 months.

Figures in the journal showed that imports of Chinese EVs rocketed from 21,000 units in 2020 to 438,000 in 2024 when tariffs were imposed.

After the tariffs were imposed, imports of EVs began to “flatten out”, with a “clear shift” from EVs to hybrids from China , it said.

Worldwide exports of hybrids from China rocketed from 191,000 vehicles in 2023 to 1.124m in 2025, the EU said.

To head off “the likelihood of substantially increased imports into the union”, the EU now is imposing a quota.

The volume limits are “safeguard” measures that have to apply to all big exporters of ‌hybrid cars to the EU. Other countries to which the import caps apply are South Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Serbia and the US, but they are most restrictive for China.

According to industry reports, non-EU countries including the UK have questioned the allocations.

At a WTO goods council meeting last week, South Korea questioned whether the investigation was fair and transparent. Japan, the UK, Switzerland and Turkey stressed transparency and due process.

China’s commerce ministry said it hoped the EU would abide by the consensus the two sides had reached, and that it reserved all rights to firmly safeguard the legitimate interests of Chinese industries.

The European Commission said imports from China came not just at the expense of EU production, but were also eating into the market shares of other exporters such as Japan and South Korea.

The UK is still fighting against a 10% tariff on all exports of EVs to the EU, due to come into force on 1 January under the 2020 Brexit trade and cooperation deal. The issue has now been intrinsically linked to Andy Burnham’s attempts to get the UK classified as a European manufacturer in the EU’s still-to-be-finalised “Made in Europe” scheme , which protects against cheap Chinese imports.

Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?

Published 25 November 2026

After the AI chipmaker Nvidia announced it was bringing back embattled former head Jensen Huang and the company's stock shot up like a bullet, President Donald Trump took a very public victory lap.

"I made the deal," he said during a lengthy phone interview with cable business news channel CNBC.

Trump followed that with an AI-generated image posted to his social media platform that riffed on the famous photograph taken moments after the 2024 attempt on his life in Pennsylvania. But instead of Trump in the image, Huang was the one surrounded by Secret Service guards. It depicted him in front of an Nvidia banner - with a raised fist clenching a red bra.

The post was classic Trump – potentially offensive, yet still a bit opaque.

Was Trump suggesting Huang survived a scandal – one that includes allegations of recklessly jeopardising US national security by consorting with a suspected Chinese spy – the way he had survived an assassin's bullet?

Was the bra a celebration Huang's reported extramarital affairs? By replacing the US flag with an Nvidia standard, was he claiming that America and one of its largest, most powerful companies are one and the same?

At the very least, the image underscores how inextricably linked Huang and Trump now are, with the fate of the former hinging on the successes and failures of the latter.

And with that comes significant risks for the American president and for Republicans, including Vice-President JD Vance, who played a key part in his efforts to rescue Huang.

While Trump has said that a "very thorough investigation" by federal officials "exonerated" Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, that is far from the final word on the matter.

"Every time you have a Chinese woman that's good looking or beautiful, they say she's a spy," Trump told CNBC, adding that "with Jensen, I don't believe that's true".

Democrats and some concerned Republicans in Congress have a different view.

They are promising to launch their own oversight of Huang and Nvidia, with subpoenas and compelled witness testimony, in order to assess whether they violated laws by allowing China to access sophisticated microchip technology.

State governments could also launch their own investigations.

Any new revelations could further damage the company's standing – and, by association, Trump himself.

"I have warned the administration from the start about Communist China obtaining our most advanced chips through both smuggling and remote access," Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted on X.

"Congress has much to investigate," he said.

Faisal Islam: Fears over the AI boom haven't gone away Published 1 day ago

What Jensen Huang's return teaches China's Xi about Trump Published 1 day ago

US attorney general dodges questions about Nvidia investigation Published 20 hours ago

While Huang has a long record of success at Nvidia, there is no guarantee that he can recapture past glory now that his star his dimmed.

Even if he is free from any criminal liability, the tech mogul is about to be in a much harsher spotlight than he has ever experienced.

Trump also appears to be on the wrong side of public opinion when it comes to AI writ large.

In the recent US midterm elections, candidates on both the left and right campaigned on imposing new restrictions on data centre construction, with many calling for new legal guardrails to prevent AI-fuelled economic and social disruption.

"Rather than addressing the American people's growing concerns about AI, this administration remains asleep at the wheel or willfully ignorant as our most advanced technologies fall into the hands of our greatest competitors," congresswoman Sydney Kamlager-Dove, a California Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the BBC.

The president's own political base is also suspicious of the new technology, with rural conservatives often rebelling at the demands that big tech companies have placed on their local resources and civic infrastructure.

How Nvidia is reacting to Jensen Huang's return as CEO

The Nvidia story has also exposed rifts in Trump's own administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a vocal proponent of AI, publicly feuding over whether to impose new restrictions on AI chip exports.

Both Bessent and Lutnick travelled with Trump on his recent trip to China, although it was the commerce secretary who hitched a ride back to the White House on the Marine One helicopter when Trump returned to Washington last Thursday.

Polling also indicated that political corruption was a top issue for voters this year.

The president's willingness to intervene in the deliberations of a major private company in which he owns millions of dollars of stock could further fuel those concerns.

Trump's decision to help save Huang – noting on Monday that "we have to protect our geniuses, and he certainly is a genius" – could further inflame the public's sense that the rich and powerful, genius or not, play by a different set of rules.

"It almost feels like they've bent the rule, the regulation, to allow this to happen because it's such an important part of our economy right now," Steve Bannon, a former top Trump adviser, said on his podcast on Monday.

"Even in the crash of 2008... I never saw the government step in and take over a board of directors."

For this American president, however, these risks appear to be worth taking because of the stakes involved.

Trump has long viewed the success of the US economy as a key part of his political legacy.

He boasted of the historic growth and low unemployment during his first presidential term (while glossing over the disruptions caused by the Covid pandemic).

And since returning to office, he has celebrated as major US stock indices posted new record highs.

Recent US economic expansion has been fuelled largely by investment in AI technology, and Trump has become one of the industry's biggest boosters.

He scolded states and local governments for blocking data centre construction and predicted that the nation that wins the race for supremacy in AI – which he has tried to rebrand as "super intelligence" – will control the fate of the world.

If Trump views the economy as the key to his political success and AI as instrumental to the health of the US economy, then his dramatic, precedent-shattering actions to try to rescue Nvidia, the company at the centre of America's AI industry, make more sense.

In the weeks since concerns over Huang's affair with a suspected Chinese spy first surfaced, Nvidia's stock price tumbled more than 32%.

Last Friday alone, it fell 14%.

US stock indices tumbled as well, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq down 10% last week and the larger S&P 500 dropping 8.6%.

The recent financial turmoil may have given Trump a glimpse into a future where AI growth is just the latest financial bubble – like the housing market in 2008 and internet companies in 2001 – that is due for a resounding pop, with similarly dire economic consequences to follow.

Trump's intervention on behalf of Huang arrested that drop, at least for a day.

On Tuesday, Nvidia's stock price gave back much of the bounce it had enjoyed, and larger stock indices were mixed. The fate of the America economy and the AI juggernaut that has powered it is still undetermined.

Trump's intervention may not be a crisis fully averted, but only a crisis delayed.

And if an AI reckoning does come, the US president will be hard-pressed to avoid being caught in the maelstrom.

stories.body:
CEO behind Nvidia’s meteoric rise stepped down after it was revealed he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, then was reinstated days later

Jensen Huang stepped down as CEO of Nvidia , the company at the center of the AI boom, after leading it for more than 30 years. The announcement of his resignation came on 12 November. A week and a half later, he was reinstated as the chief executive in a unanimous vote by Nvidia’s board.

Huang, an electrical engineer by education, stewarded the company from a $1bn firm when it went public in 1999 to a company valued at more than $4tn in 2026. But in a matter of days, after it was revealed he had an extramarital affair with a woman that US officials believe to be a Chinese spy, Huang managed to wipe more than $600bn from the company’s valuation.

China has denied the accusations that it had tapped Alice Huang, the woman in question and a top executive at a datacenter company called Megaspeed, to be an intelligence asset, and called them a “smear”. US officials had reportedly started to monitor the Megaspeed executive after suspecting the firm was diverting powerful Nvidia AI chips to Chinese firms, in potential violation of export restrictions. The Biden and Trump administrations had prohibited US companies from exporting some of the more powerful AI chips to China over national security concerns.

Initially, it seemed that Huang’s ouster was unlikely, but in the days since he first disclosed an affair and affirmed his commitment to the company, the New York Times reported that there was a second affair – this time with another Nvidia executive. Reuters later reported a third affair, this one with another Nvidia employee.

How did we get here? Here’s a timeline of what we know about Huang’s entanglements.

2023

March 2023 Megaspeed, a datacenter firm, is spun out from a Chinese video game company

Megaspeed is the datacenter firm at the center of the spy allegations. Before it was its own company, it was a part of one of China’s largest video game companies, 7Road Holdings Ltd . At this time, Megaspeed was controlled by a firm called Huang Le Ltd, an entity affiliated with Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg.

November 2023 Megaspeed is sold to a Singaporean shell company and becomes an Nvidia cloud partner

Huang Le Ltd sells its shares of Megaspeed to a Singaporean shell company called Swiftdata. The sale comes weeks after Joe Biden issued an executive order limiting investment in China’s AI industry.

Soon after, Megaspeed is designated an Nvidia cloud partner, which means the company could get preferential access to Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

2024

June 2024 Alice Huang and Jensen Huang are seen together in Taipei, Taiwan

Jensen Huang is seen with Alice Huang at a bar in Taipei where several AI industry executives had gathered . The person who introduced them to each other was Alice Huang’s husband , Kang Wei, who had worked with her on several business ventures, according to the Wall Street Journal.

2024 to 2025 Megaspeed receives hundreds of shipments of Nvidia AI chips

The Singapore-based firm fields 200 shipments of AI chips, according to the New York Times . The company then rents out compute power, which is fueled by these AI chips, to major companies including the Chinese firms Tencent and Alibaba.

September 2024 The US Department of Commerce begins investigating Megaspeed

The commerce department begins investigating whether Megaspeed is diverting Nvidia chips to Chinese firms, according to the New York Times. This could violate export restrictions on advanced AI chips.

2025

January 2025 Jensen Huang meets Donald Trump for the first time

Huang visits Donald Trump in the weeks after he takes office.

April 2025 Jensen Huang attends a dinner for donors at Mar-a-Lago

The dinner costs $1m a person and the president briefly puts a pause on imposing restrictions on Nvidia chip sales to China. The restriction is ultimately implemented shortly after.

May 2025 Jensen Huang is again seen with Alice Huang

The two attend an industry conference in Taiwan. The New York Times also reports that Alice Huang visited the Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California, two months earlier.

October 2025 Trump is reportedly briefed on the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang

The New York Times reports in October 2025 that intelligence officials told Trump that the two had a relationship and alleged that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Trump chose not to take action, according to the Times report. Trump has since said at a White House press conference that he didn’t remember being briefed on this.

December 2025 Trump approves the sale of more advanced Nvidia chips to China

Trump grants Nvidia permission to sell its second-most powerful chips to China. A portion of the sales would go to the US government.

2026

May 2026 Marco Rubio reportedly drafts a memo about Jensen Huang and Alice Huang

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, drafts the memo based on information gleaned from electronic surveillance of Alice Huang, according to the New York Times. The memo warns that Jensen Huang has become close to an alleged Chinese spy. Trump still invites Huang on his trip to China, saying in a social media post that he is honored to have “the Great Jensen Huang” on the trip.

October 2026 The New York Times reports Jensen Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese spy

At the time, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo says Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang is nothing out of the ordinary.

8 November 2026 Jensen Huang admits to having an affair

In a letter to employees, Huang says that he had an extramarital affair, apologizes to his family and reaffirms his commitment to the company. The Nvidia board says it is investigating the relationship but has no reason to believe national security secrets or company secrets were divulged. “The board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” members of the Board say in a statement.

Silicon Valley leaders rally behind him , and at the time it appears that Huang might hang on to his job, despite his image being tarnished .

9 November 2026 Trump says he is ‘amazed’ by the allegations that Alice Huang is a spy

At a press conference , Trump says the FBI is investigating Jensen Huang but adds that he thinks Huang will be “in good shape”.

“And I asked him about that, and he … said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy,” the president says at a press conference. “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’

“I really believe him,” Trump says.

10 November 2026 A shareholder in California files a lawsuit against Nvidia and its CEO

Retail investor Mark Kistenmacher files a lawsuit accusing the company of misleading investors over Huang’s affair, claiming that Nvidia did not disclose the situation and raised national security concerns that could threaten the company’s business prospects.

11 November 2026 The New York Times reports there was a second affair, and the Nvidia board reportedly prepares to oust Huang

The New York Times reports that Huang also allegedly had an affair with the company’s vice-president of healthcare.

At this point things are looking precarious for Jensen Huang, and then the Wall Street Journal reports that the Nvidia board is preparing to oust the CEO.

12 November 2026 Jensen Huang steps down as CEO of Nvidia

Huang steps down, effectively ending his 33-year tenure leading the company he co-founded in 1993. The board starts a search for the company’s next CEO while the company’s chief finance officer, Colette Kress, serves as interim CEO.

Meanwhile, shares in the company continue to plummet.

17 November 2026 Nvidia’s board says it will not reinstate Jensen Huang

Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chair of the company’s board says. Harvey Jones makes the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announces the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago.

23 November 2026 Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia’s CEO

Nvidia reinstates Huang as chief executive in a stunning reversal. The company’s shares surge on the news, jumping 33% and adding more than $1tn to its market value.

Donald Trump, who had called for Huang’s return, trumpets his own involvement in negotiations with Nvidia’s board to return the former CEO to his position. The president says, “the country needs Jensen’s leadership” and that the US government has no “evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct”.

In a statement , the board says it “believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers”.

stories.title: Disability benefit review calls for closer link with claimant costs
stories.summary: A government-commissioned report calls for a "rebalancing" of the amount paid to different claimants.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

The main disability benefit in England and Wales should be more closely linked to the additional costs claimants face, a government-commissioned review has recommended.

The review on personal independence payment (Pip) led by Disability Minister Sir Stephen Timms said the current system was "not appropriate" for claimants who do not have any extra costs arising from their condition.

The government has committed to some of its recommendations, including fast-track payments for people with severe conditions, but will not respond fully to the plans until early next year.

The Conservatives said the year-long review was a "compete farce" and showed a "complete absence of substance".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately added: "All we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system".

Pip is available to people with long-term physical or mental health conditions who have difficulty doing every day tasks, regardless of whether they work, and it is not linked to income or savings.

The number of people claiming Pip in England and Wales has roughly doubled since 2019 to around four million.

The Timms review was set up last year by Sir Keir Starmer's government after his aborted attempt to cut welfare spending, which was derailed by the threat of a rebellion by Labour MPs.

It was co-produced with groups representing disabled people, who had a role in drafting the report.

Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit Published 1 day ago

Giving a statement in the House of Commons, Sir Stephen said Pip "remains a vital source of support" but the system was "no longer fit for purpose".

He told MPs the current assessment process was "dehumanising" and focused on "what somebody cannot do", rather than "supporting independence".

The government has committed to a recommendation that people receiving end-of-life care or with "serious, well-evidenced conditions" would receive payments without a full assessment.

It has also agreed to reduce "unnecessary" reviews for people whose conditions are lifelong or unlikely to improve.

Under the report's proposals, cash payments would remain alongside better support to signpost people into education or employment, although claimants could choose to exchange part of their payment for practical services instead.

In the longer-term, the report recommends changes to the assessment process that look at someone's real-life additional costs and individual needs, focusing on "how people can live the life they want to live, rather than what they cannot do".

It proposes "improved" questions to understand the extra costs people face, although claimants would not be asked to calculate their costs or provide receipts.

'Rebalancing'

Currently eligibility for Pip is based on how difficult people find carrying out everyday tasks, with two levels of payment available.

But the review suggests future payment options could include bands more closely linked to extra costs.

The report says its approach is likely to lead to a "rebalancing" of payments, indicating that some claimants could lose out under a new system, either receiving less than they do currently or not qualifying for payments at all.

"Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support," it says.

"Conversely, this benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled."

The review also calls for an increase in face-to-face assessments, which has been show to reduce eligibility.

The remit of the review was not to produce savings, and it does not set out whether the reforms would reduce the overall welfare bill.

Spending on Pip is set to be about £32bn this financial year, a figure projected to rise to £41.5bn by the end of the decade.

It comes after a separate review by former minister Alan Milburn into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets).

The government welcomed Milburn's report , which included a recommendation to move under-25s off Pip and the health element of universal credit, and onto an entirely new benefits system.

This has led to concerns about a two-tier system, where some people with the same conditions could get different levels of payments depending on their age.

The government has said it will consider the Timms review alongside Milburn's recommendations, with its final proposals set out early next year.

Sir Stephen said this would include detailing the overall costs of changes to the system.

At a glance: Key proposals from Milburn's Neets report Published 17 November

'Months of uncertainty'

Eduin Latimer, senior research economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, said the review's recommendations had "the potential to better tailor Pip to claimants' needs".

But he said this would also create challenges, "most importantly in defining what disability-related costs are included, and finding a fair way of measuring them".

Latimer said making it easier to apply for Pip in its current form would "likely increase the number of claimants - and hence spending".

He added: "If the government wants to make Pip easier to apply for while also keeping spending in line with current projections, they would likely have to tighten eligibility criteria or reduce award amounts."

Disability charities have largely welcomed the review's recommendations of fast-tracked support and fewer reassessments.

However, they have said any changes should not leave disabled people financially worse off.

The Liberal Democrats said younger disabled people would now face "months of uncertainty" whilst the government considers the separate reviews from Timms and Milburn, and urged ministers to say quickly what they intend to do.

Reform UK's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said: "Timms' recommendations will not cut the ballooning benefits bill so taxes on working people will inevitably rise."

He said his party would "bring back rigorous in-person assessments and ensure benefits are only available for British people" in order to lower the welfare bill.

The disability benefit system is devolved in Scotland and will not change in line with England and Wales. However, the Timms Review could impact the funding the Scottish government receives.

Disability benefits are also devolved in Northern Ireland, but in practice it reflects any changes made to the system in England and Wales.

stories.summary: Senedd members reject Reform's motion to oust Huw Irranca Davies by 55 votes to 29.

stories.body:
Huw Irranca-Davies gave a passionate speech to the Senedd in defence of his role

Published 24 November 2026

An attempt by Reform UK to remove the Senedd's presiding officer has failed, following a passionate speech to the Welsh Parliament by Huw Irranca-Davies.

Members of the Senedd (MSs) rejected Reform's motion by 55 votes to 29.

Earlier the party ended a two-week boycott of most proceedings in the chamber after one of them, Joe Martin, was banned from speaking and told to apologise for remarks about immigration.

Irranca-Davies, whose title is Llywydd, said his duty was to "apply the rules fairly and impartially".

Reform's Llyr Powell said: "If you had a problem with what Joe Martin said, debate him, don't shut him down."

A source close to Irranca-Davies had "wholly refuted" Reform's accusations he had changed his mind during negotiations about Martin returning to the debating chamber.

Irranca-Davies had ruled that a claim by Martin - that white people were being "replaced" - broke the rules because it was "unnecessarily provocative and deliberately offensive".

Responding to Reform's attempt to remove him on Tuesday evening, the presiding office gave a long and passionate speech in defence of his role, which prompted a standing ovation from the other Cardiff Bay parties.

"The duty of the chair is not to please, it is not to flatter, not to avoid controversy, it is to apply the rules fairly and impartially, irrespective of pressure, of popularity or of political consequence," he said.

"Parliamentary privilege has never meant that anything goes, it has never meant speech without standards, it has never meant rights without responsibilities.

"Without rules, eventually it is only the loudest voices that are heard, without rules intimidation begins to replace persuasion, without rules scrutiny deteriorates into shouting."

After losing the vote, which Reform had no realistic prospect of winning, its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said it was "now clear that the establishment parties are content to see a Member of this Senedd silenced".

"We will continue to fight for the rights of elected members to represent their constituents as they see fit," she said.

Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon

At the start of the afternoon session, without announcing an end to their protest, Reform MSs walked into the debating chamber together ahead of First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon. Martin was not among them.

Jenner began her contribution by asking Senedd members: "Did you miss us?

"It's been a little bit duller without us in here."

In an answer to a question from her, First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said "it's good of her to turn up today", and later accused her party of "chucking their toys out of the pram".

Reform is the biggest opposition group in the Senedd, but its members have stayed away from plenary sessions - full meetings in the debating chamber - since 11 November .

The party said it had left its seats empty during debates and questions to Welsh government ministers because it was standing up for free speech.

The boycott began after Irranca-Davies told Martin his comments had broken the Senedd's rules, and he would not be called to speak until he apologised.

Reform's Welsh leader Helen Jenner attempted to force the Senedd's presiding officer to quit

Shortly after its members had returned to the Senedd chamber, the party sent journalists a statement from Jenner.

She said the party "thought we were approaching a sensible resolution" in talks with the Llywydd that would allow Martin "to return to the chamber without apologising for the speech he made in the Senedd".

"It has become clear this morning that the Llywydd has not been negotiating in good faith and has changed his mind at the eleventh hour," Jenner said.

"He has admitted to us that his decisions on this matter have been influenced by the feelings of outside organisations.

"It is now for him to explain to the people of Wales which organisations they are and what that means for Welsh democracy.

"We now have no choice but to escalate this situation."

The Senedd's authorities strongly denied Reform's "completely inaccurate" claims and said the Llywydd's position had remained the same since he ruled against Martin.

A source close to Irranca-Davies said he was "always clear" during four meetings with Reform that Martin needed to apologise.

Irranca-Davies, who chairs Senedd plenary sessions, left the chamber during First Minister's Questions on Tuesday afternoon.

A spokesperson for the Llywydd said he met Jenner "entirely in good faith and had hoped to continue these confidential discussions constructively".

"It is unfortunate that they have chosen this course of action," the spokesperson added.

"While the Llywydd is disappointed, he respects the democratic process.

"Just as members elected him to this role, it is right that they have the opportunity to decide whether he continue to have their confidence."

stories.body:
Accused official leaked national secrets to unnamed country and received payments worth over $150,000, state-linked publisher says

A Chinese official has been sentenced to death for spying for a foreign country, a government-linked publisher has said.

Gold Wall Press, a publishing company associated with China’s national administration of state secrets protection, said the convicted person was surnamed Ma and was approached and recruited by an unnamed foreign intelligence service while working abroad.

Chinese courts typically do not publish information about state security cases, but in recent years the powerful ministry of state security and Gold Wall Press have increasingly publicised arrests, as well as using social media, movies and comics to promote warnings about espionage.

The statement on Monday said Ma had signed a cooperation agreement containing clauses on “confidentiality” and “loyalty” and received fixed monthly payments. In total, it said, he provided 35 pieces of information that were classified as national secrets and received payments worth more than 1m yuan ($150,000).

An intelligence operative identified as Kailin “frequently arranged to meet with Ma, hoping to engage with him more”, citing an interest in learning Chinese, the statement said. Kailin later introduced him to a colleague who threatened to report his earlier disclosures to Chinese authorities if he refused to cooperate.

After returning to China, Ma continued to gather intelligence for the foreign agency, which provided him with a laptop, the statement said. He used his position to collect material from classified documents during the day and transmitted it overseas at night via an espionage website.

The statement did not identify the countries involved, or say when or where he was sentenced or whether he had already been executed.

The case comes as US intelligence has been publicising its own efforts to recruit sources in China. The five most-viewed videos on the CIA’s YouTube channel are recruiting advertisements in Mandarin.

“This shocking case serves as yet another wake-up call,” the Gold Wall Press said, warning that foreign intelligence agencies were “cunning” and used emotional ties, financial interests and threats to recruit people in key positions.

The statement also urged officials to remain vigilant, strengthen their loyalty to the Communist party, protect state secrets and guard against foreign recruitment.

In 2023 Beijing broadened its anti-espionage law, expanding the definition of espionage and strengthening the investigative powers of state security authorities. The following year it revised its state secrets law to extend restrictions on sensitive information to so-called “work secrets”.

stories.title: Key takeaways from the Timms review into Pip disability benefit
stories.summary: Disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has published his review of the personal independence payment (Pip), along with recommended changes.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 24 November 2026

A review of the main disability benefit has recommended an overhaul of the system to allow disabled people to "achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence".

The report proposes both short and long terms changes to the personal independence payment (Pip) for claimants in England and Wales.

The benefit is claimed by four million people and is available to people whether they are in work or unemployed. Its aim is to help with the additional costs of being disabled.

Here's what you need to know.

Pip benefit system 'not fit for purpose' and 'dehumanising' assessments should change, review finds - follow live

The current Pip process does not work

This is the first review of the benefit since it was introduced in 2013. More than 40,000 disabled people engaged with the process with more than 90% of them saying they'd had a negative experience while applying for Pip, describing it as stressful, dehumanising or psychologically damaging. The review concludes the Pip process is "not fit for purpose" and calls for a fundamental redesign.

While the review was chaired by Sir Stephen Timms, the disability minister, the experience of disabled people is clear throughout the review.

The review recommends both short and long term changes

First the short term.

A fast-track process should be introduced for two types of claimants.

Those with terminal illnesses should get the fastest route to an award to ensure their lives are as comfortable as possible.

Those who have severe conditions that are well-evidenced and unlikely to change over time, and whose impact on daily living is clear, should also receive the benefit without a full assessment. Any subsequent review should avoid unnecessary reassessments.

Then the long term.

Other claimants will have to go through an updated initial assessment. This will examine how a person's condition affects their daily life – functions, barriers, and needs that are currently not being met. This assessment will determine entitlement to the benefit. It will also decide the level of cash award, which will remain the bedrock of the benefit.

Optional referrals to support services should also be offered but this will be voluntary and a refusal to engage with them should not affect the benefit level.

A new set of questions should be developed to better understand the extra costs a person faces, but will not ask them to calculate costs or provide receipts. The system should recognise fluctuating and cumulative needs and produce decisions that are consistent and be robust against misuse.

The 28-day hospitalisation rule – which sees Pip payments suspended if someone spends more than 28 days as an inpatient – should also be reviewed as claimants find it can cause unnecessary stress and can delay discharges from hospitals.

The review does not propose benefits cuts

The inquiry was not set up to find savings in the system despite the fact that spending on Pip is forecast to cost more than £40bn by 2030. In the year before the Covid pandemic, Pip cost £16.3bn when adjusted for inflation to today's prices.

The report acknowledges that since the benefit was introduced, the number of people receiving disability benefits has increased across every age group for both men and women. Most of the increase has happened between 2019 and 2024, with the sharpest increases among young people aged 16-19, people in their 30s and women, whose rates of benefit receipt have risen faster than men's.

The report says that a reformed Pip system that more accurately reflects peoples' needs will likely mean "a rebalancing process". While the review didn't set out to make savings, it couldn't increase the overall costs and with some people likely to gain, others will almost certainly lose some cash. The review is not explicit on who these people might be.

Separate research last month from a think tank, the Resolution Foundation, suggested that one in six Pip recipients didn't have any additional costs associated with their conditions. In an interview to coincide with the review, Timms said that "if people don't have extra costs, then this is not the benefit for them".

How does this report sit with the Milburn review that was published last week?

Alan Milburn's report - which proposed widespread changes to help get young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) into work across the UK - recommended that Pip be removed from people under 25 as part of a package of measures to tackle youth unemployment.

Today's review does not make the same recommendation. It will be up to the government to decide how they marry the two reports. They have said they are committed to reforming the Pip assessment process, but what that means in practice probably won't be known until the New Year when they publish their considered response.

stories.title: Tory plan to sell off London's Victorian jails to raise £1.4bn
stories.summary: The party says the move could fund the construction of modern purpose-built prisons elsewhere.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Wandsworth prison, in south London, is among those that would be closed by the Conservatives

Published 24 November 2026

London's Victorian jails should be closed down and the land sold off to property developers, the Conservatives have said, as they launched a plan to massively increase prison places in England and Wales.

Shadow justice secretary Nick Timothy said the move could raise £1.4bn to help fund the construction of "modern, purpose-built prisons elsewhere".

He claimed a Tory government would create 50,000 extra prison places within "six or seven years" and end Labour's early release scheme in its first term in office.

Labour said nobody would believe the Tory plan "given they only added a dismal 500 places while in government".

Speaking at a press conference in Westminster, Timothy said it was "fair" to highlight the previous Conservartive government's failure to significantly increase prison places.

But he insisted "this is a different generation of Conservative politicians under Kemi [Badenoch]'s leadership, and we are making different choices".

Unlike previous Tory-led administrations, they were being "explicit" about which departmental budgets they would cut - international aid, culture and the Cabinet Office - to fund new prisons, he added.

Under the Tory plans, an extra £2bn a year would go to the Ministry of Justice to pay for what Timothy called "the largest prison-building programme in modern history".

"It will let us end Labour's early release schemes once and for all, and bring back shorter sentences to lock up criminals like shoplifters," he added.

He told the audience "prison works" because it kept criminals off the street and he was "deeply sceptical about talk of rehabilitation".

The Conservatives are setting up a commission, chaired by former minister Sir Simon Clarke, to work out how to speed up the building of new prisons by removing obstacles in the planning, procurement and judicial systems.

The review would also look at "how to get out of the old Victorian prison estate, starting in London," Timothy said in his speech.

Prisons such as Wormwood Scrubs, Brixton, Wandsworth and Pentonville "sit on some of the most valuable land in the world," he added.

"Getting out of these sites is not only a good idea in itself. It will free up land for residential use in London, where our housing shortage is most acute."

He said the Tories would "strip back regulations, like affordable housing quotas and listed status, to give the land its highest realisable value," but it would only sell off the land when "market conditions are favourable to the taxpayer".

This could raise more than £1.4bn which would go towards building new prisons "in addition to" the 50,000 places the party has already pledged to build , he added.

The previous Conservative government set out plans to sell off London's Victorian jails, but this was ditched by Boris Johnson's administration in 2019 because of the shortage of prison places.

A Labour spokesperson said: "When it comes to leaving the prisons estate on the verge of collapse, the Tories are guilty as charged.

"They should be apologising to victims of crime who they badly let down rather than spending time lecturing others who are fixing the mess they left behind."

The Labour government was "delivering the largest prison building programme since the Victorian era so victims of crime get the justice they deserve," they added.

stories.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
stories.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services

Published 12 minutes ago

US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

stories.title: Signal Moves to Block AI Agents
stories.summary: Signal announced an update to its mobile apps on iOS and Android that seeks to curb issues with AI agents accessing private chats. This is a useful new barrier against a problem we’ve been highlighting this year in our Encrypt It Already campaign. And good news, it’s enabled by default so you don’t need to do anything except update the app. Over the last year, both Google and Apple* have released AI features in their operating systems that can read the contents of apps. One of the ways it can do this is through screen analysis. Google calls this feature “ Intelligent Screen Context ,” while Apple refers to it as either “ Onscreen Awareness ” or “ Visual Intelligence .” Apple now provides a way to block Siri AI’s access to apps, but by default every app is available to Siri AI, so it’s up to the user to go in and put these guardrails up. Signal requests that protection on your behalf. Google doesn’t currently offer any sort of similar option. So Signal on Android does the best it can, by turning off screenshots when it detects an AI assistant attempting to access the screen. Signal’s solution helps ensure that, unless you go in and change the setting yourself, it defaults to the most private option. While this is a clever solution to the current issues facing Signal (and potentially useful for any other app that does its best to promise privacy), we need all operating systems to provide stronger methods and clear documentation to developers so they can safeguard their users without needing to jump through hoops. Both developers and users should have the tools they need to safeguard their own data from AI agents and other AI tools. *Apple is an EFF donor. EFF donors do not influence our agenda or our positions.
